. Freelance 
workers, subcontractors, agencies, consultants 
and 
the self-employed are examples of outsourced workers; 
they are hired by an organization for their expertise. For 
instance, most large firms use marketing agencies to design 
appropriate promotional campaigns (see Chapter 29).

subject: Business Management
content:
The three parts of the Shamrock Organization have their own 
advantages and limitations for a business. The core workers, 
vital to the organization, must be well paid and remunerated. 
They are likely to enjoy some degree of job security, be highly 
motivated and very productive. The peripheral workers 
will suffer from a lack of job security thereby negatively 
affecting their morale. However, they present flexibility for an 
organization and are easier to 'hire and fire'. The outsourced 
workers are experts in their fields but are therefore likely to be 
relatively expensive. 
Although Handy introduced the idea of the Shamrock 
Organization back in the early 1990s, time has shown that 
businesses are indeed restructuring to become more flexible 
in their organizational structures, reducing the core staff and 
opting to use more peripheral and outsourced workers. The 
trend in the number of businesses globally that use increasingly 
more part-time workers and adopt flexible working practices 
supports Handy's foresight. 
Organizational structure and the key 
concepts 
Human resources are undoubtedly essential to any business 
organization, given their creativity potential and changes in 
the internal and external business environments

subject: Business Management
content:
. Effective 
organization of people requires careful strategic human 
resource planning (see Chapter 7). An organization chart is an 
important aspect of strategic planning as it allows people to see: 
• 
The overall structure of human resources in the organization 
Each manger's scope of responsibility 
Those who must report to a certain line manager 
The formal chains of command. 
An inefficient organizational structure can cause staff 
demotivation, a duplication of effort, communication problems, 
difficulties in coordination and poor decision-making. Hence, 
organization charts can be useful visual tools for the process of 
change and change management. 
As an organization evolves and grows, it is inevitable that 
change will create new job roles as well as make other roles 
redundant. The increased need for human resources in 
creative and flexible ways means that managers may have to 
restructure the organization as part of their overall strategic 
plan. For example, tall structures, which were popularised 
2.2 Organizational structure 
in the 1930s, have given way to flatter structures in many 
large organizations today. Delayering not only cuts costs and 
unnecessary management roles (financial rewards for managers 
are typically based on their hierarchical rank), but also leads to 
more effective communications (see Chapter 12)

subject: Business Management
content:
. Delegation of 
decision-making authority is also pushed down and spread out 
amongst those lower in the hierarchy. As a result, productivity 
should improve. For example, Japanese companies found that 
the strategic implementation of matrix structures and quality 
circles (see Chapter 37) creates synergy, thereby improving 
their overall efficiency and competitiveness and in a more 
sustainable way. However, overseas expansion also means that 
managers have to be aware of potential cultural differences (see 
Chapter 11) and approaches to organizational structures. 
Although there has been extensive research into the optimal 
organizational structure, the conclusion is that there simply 
isn't a model that suits all organizations. Each model has its own 
strengths and weaknesses and every organization is unique in 
its character, code of ethics and culture. The 'best' or optimal 
strategy depends on several key factors, including: 
The size of the business - Larger organizations tend to 
require more formal structures. 
Employee competencies - Organizations with highly skilled 
workers can adopt relatively flat, flexible or project-based 
structures, whereas those with low-skilled workers require 
a more formal and rigorous structure

subject: Business Management
content:
. 
Management attitudes - Managers who are able to trust 
their staff and are willing to relinquish or delegate decision-
making power are more likely to implement flatter and 
flexible work structures. 
The culture of the organization - Creative and innovative 
organizations that are accustomed to change, for example, 
might opt for more flexible, project-based structures. 
In today's fast-paced business environment, where change 
is unavoidable, flexibility is a key feature of an organization's 
business strategy. Since many decisions and actions need to 
be spontaneous, the decision-making process can no longer 
be heavily centralized. For example, if firms choose to adopt 
Handy's Shamrock Organization, then the internal structure of 
the business needs to be reviewed. This often leads to delayering 
caused by downsizing (when the size of the core workforce in 
the Shamrock Organization is reduced). This strategy can lead 
to more flexible working practises (see Chapter 7) as firms hire 
more peripheral and temporary workers. These people are not

Scientific and intuitive thinking/

S
cientific thinking and management are based on 
objectivity, facts and empirical evidence. It follows a 
formal and prescribed procedure. Decisions are based on 
quantifiable data and proof rather than on subjective opinions, 
emotions, or intuition. The main benefit of scientific decision 
making is that decisions are made rationally and logically. This 
means that decisions are simpler to justify (as they are based on 
factual evidence) and easier to communicate to the staff. It can 
also reduce the risks involved in taking a particular decision. 
By contrast, intuitive thinking and management is based 
on personal beliefs, perceptions and instincts or gut feelings. 
It considers issues that are not necessarily quantifiable, such 
as the impact of strategic decisions on the well-being of 
employees and the effects on the local community, or whether 
the decisions are morally correct

subject: Business Management
content:
. Intuitive decision making is 
quicker and less expensive than scientific decision making. As

based on their intuition. This might be due to a lack of time 
to collect and analyse the necessary data and evidence, or due

be higher, only highly experienced managers tend to use this 
approach. 
In reality, most decisions are based on a combination of both 
scientific and intuitive aspects. The business environment is 
dynamic in nature and decisions taken in the past that proved 
successful may not be so effective in the current environment 
or future situations. The choice of decision making depends on 
numerous factors, both scientific and intuitive. For example: 
Highly successful senior managers can make lots of 
intuitive decisions based on their acquired knowledge and 
past managerial experiences. 
Less experienced managers may, however, feel that they 
need evidence to support their decision making.

Management and leadership 
(A02) 
"Management is doing things right; leadership is doing the 
right things." 
- Peter F. Drucker (1909 - 2005), management 
consultant, educator and author 
Mary Parker Follett ( 1868 - 1933) famously defined management 
as "the art of getting things done through people:• Management 
is essentially about problem-solving and decision-making, so 
involves a process of planning, organizing and coordinating 
resources to achieve organizational objectives

subject: Business Management
content:
. Therefore, 
management is the practice of achieving an organization's 
objectives by using and controlling the available human and 
non-human resources of the business in an effective way. A 
manager is someone with decision-making authority within an 
organization and has responsibility for problem solving in order 
to achieve specific organizational goals. Managers tend to focus 
on achieving specific organizational goals within a definite time 
frame. The functions of management are outlined in Box 9.1. 
132

subject: Business Management
content:
MAN AGER 
Figure 9.2 - A manager has decision-making authority 
Leadership is the process of influencing, invigorating and 
inspiring others to achieve organizational goals. A leader is 
someone who influences and inspires others to get things done. 
A leader fosters motivation, respect, trust and loyalty from the 
workforce. Leaders tend to focus on achieving broader goals or 
visions, with no definitive time frame in mind. 
The terms management and leadership are often used 
interchangeably because they serve similar purposes. At 
times, this is acceptable. However, there are some significant 
differences and it is important to consider these when referring 
specifically to either management or leadership: 
Time and devotion - Management is sometimes described 
as a '9am to 5 pm' job, whereas leadership is about being 
responsible 24-hours each day. Professor Warren Bennis 
(1925 - 2014) argues that managers have a short-term view 
2.3 Leadership and management 
followers through action and a vision. Leaders focus on 
people rather than concentrating on tasks. Hence, leaders 
are more socially engaged than managers. Bennis claims 
the key to competitiveness rests with the ability of leaders 
to generate intellectual capital (the skills and competencies 
of the workforce)

subject: Business Management
content:
. This means that people can no longer be 
seen as resources that are simply managed as this would 
be "as difficult as herding cats" - a phrase that means it is 
impossible to manage the unmanageable. Instead, leaders 
inspire and entrust creative and talented people to help 
develop the organization. 
Risk taking - Managers follow predetermined rules and 
policies set by the organization. They tackle a particular task 
by keeping order and control, complying with company 
expectations and policies. Hence, their focus tends to be

One drawback of an autocratic leadership style is that 
communication is top-down, so any opinions or suggestions

become overly dependent on the leader and are unable to act 
on their own initiative. Hence, this leadership style can alienate 
and demotivate the workforce (see chapter 10), cause higher 
levels of staff absenteeism and increase the labour turnover rate.

subject: Business Management

leader sets the objectives, but it is up to employees to decide

This can cause high levels of motivation because the employees 
feel trusted and highly valued by their employer. Workers might 
feel that they have control over their work and can contribute to 
the success of the organization. This leadership style is suitable 
in businesses or situations where creativity is important, such 
as in computer software companies and advertising agencies. 
A key limitation of laissez-faire leadership is that coordination 
and decision-making can be time-consuming as there is a 
lack of direct supervision or support. Hence, execution of 
business strategy can be prolonged, so this leadership style is 
unsuitable for businesses or situations that require quick and 
critical decision-making. It also relies heavily on teamwork and 
the goodwill of employees to achieve the organization's goals. 
Laissez-faire leadership might also encourage a degree of slack, 
i.e. people may be less proactive if they know they are not being 
directly monitored by senior management. After all, such a 
leadership style relies heavily on trusting workers to get their 
jobs done

Situational leadership is a leadership style that, unlike the others 
above, is not based on any single dominant approach. In essence, 
it is about using the right leadership style for the right situation. 
As Mahatma Gandhi (1869 - 1948) said, "Leadership at one time 
meant muscles, but today it means getting along with people." 
For example, a crisis requires a more autocratic leadership style 
whereas a laissez-faire approach can be ordinarily adopted by 
the same leaders who have highly skilled and empowered staff. 
Situational leadership also suggests that leaders must be able to 
change and adapt their style to different situations. 'CLOTS'• is

Many businesses argue that people (human resources) are their

seek to get the most out of their human resources by using 
appropriate methods of motivation. Motivation theory looks at 
how managers seek to motivate their workforce to maximise job 
satisfaction, staff morale and labour productivity. Businesses 
need to understand what motivates people in order to achieve

(i) Taylor (1911) 
Frederick Winslow Taylor (1856 - 1915), an American engineer 
and inventor, advocated the use of piece-rate payment systems 
suggesting that "what the workmen want from employers beyond 
anything else is higher wages:' Taylor's principles of scientific 
management assumed that employees are primarily motivated 
by money and that productivity could be improved by setting 
output and efficiency targets related to pay.

Taylor believed it was a manager's duty to decide how each

"In the majority of cases, man deliberately plans to do as little

their own work but only sought to maximise their personal 
reward from work. Hence, Taylor promoted the use of division 
of labour (breaking down different aspects of a job or task 
and assigning different people to each particular part of the 
work), thus specialising in the production process to improve 
efficiency and output.

contributions of workers. It can be difficult to measure physical

only and simply motivated by money. Taylor's theory ignored

Herzberg also looked at the crucial difference between what he 
called 'movement' and what he understood to be 'motivation'. 
Movement occurs when people do something because they 
need to, perhaps because it is part of their job, so they feel 
obliged to do so. Hence, movement is an extrinsic incentive. 
By contrast, motivation happens when people do something 
because they want to, i.e. it is based on intrinsic reasons. Unlike 
other theorists who believed that people are motivated mainly 
by financial rewards, Herzberg felt that workers are motivated 
by being responsible for their work, i.e. the work itself can be 
rewarding. 
Herzberg's theory allowed managers to think in a different way 
from previous motivational theorists such as Taylor and Maslow. 
The existence of hygiene factors meant it might be better for 
managers to ensure that workers are not demotivated, rather 
than hypothesising what might motivate them

The following motivation theories are also stated in the syllabus 
for HL students: (i) McClelland's acquired needs theory, 
(ii) Deci and Ryan's self-determination and (iii) equity and

{i} McClelland's acquired needs theory 
{1961} {HL only} 
American psychologist David McClelland (1917 - 1998) put 
forward the acquired needs theory ( also known as the learned 
needs theory). From his study of 500 managers working in 25 
American companies, McClelland acknowledged that managing 
a group of people with different personalities and varying needs 
can be challenging. From his studies, McClelland concluded in 
his book, "The Achieving Society" (1961) that three types of 
needs must be satisfied to boost motivation and productivity, 
regardless of people's gender, culture or age: 
1. N eed for Achievement (n-Ach). McClelland found that 
achievement-motivated people tend to be moderate risk 
takers. Low risk activities are too easy to accomplish so 
n-Ach people do not feel they have genuinely achieved 
anything. They do not take high risks either as the outcome 
is largely based on chance and luck, rather than through 
their own efforts

subject: Business Management
content:
. These people also prefer to work on tasks 
where they hold key responsibilities or work alongside 
high achievers. They are more interested in personal 
success rather than extrinsic rewards that recognise their 
achievements. This could mean that n-Ach people prefer 
not to delegate tasks. They also tend to self-reflect on their 
performance in order to find ways to further improve. 
McClelland suggested that the major causes of n-Ach 
are parental influences, cultural factors and educational 
experiences. 
2. N eed for Power (n-Pow). Power-motivated people like 
to influence the behaviour of others so tend to be very 
strong-willed. Power can take two forms: personal or 
institutional. Those who seek personal power do so to pass 
on instructions or orders to others. Perhaps this makes 
the person feel more important, but it often makes others 
resent the individual who is seen by others as simply 'bossy' 
or even a 'power freak'. Staff will have to do as they are told, 
irrespective of whether they agree with then-Pow person 
or not. By contrast, people who have institutional power 
strive to make others work harder in order to achieve 
organizational objectives. They use their authority to try 
and bring out the best in their teams

subject: Business Management
content:
. Hence, McClelland 
argued that these people are more likely to be successful. 
He also suggested that good leaders need to have at least 
150 
moderate n-Pow as leadership is about influencing the 
behaviour of others. 
3. N eed for Affiliation (n-Aff). People who need affiliation 
seek to have a good social and working relationship with 
colleagues and the senior management team. This makes 
them happier at work, thereby increasing their motivation 
and productivity. Such people tend to conform to group 
norms and avoid conflict in order to be accepted as part of a 
group. Unlike n-Ach people who may prefer to work alone, 
n-Aff people favour opportunities for social interactions, 
such as teamworking or customer relations. 
McClelland believed that these three needs are present in all 
people although the relative intensity of each one varies from 
person to person. He helped to provide insight into how people 
with different kinds of needs are motivated in different ways. 
Managers who are aware of these acquired needs and how they 
affect employees can allocate jobs and tasks more suitably to 
boost motivation and productivity. 
In summary, employees with high n-Ach ought to be given 
challenging but achievable tasks

subject: Business Management

. People with high n-Pow could 
be given opportunities to manage and lead different teams of 
people. Finally, those with n-Aff should be provided with a 
cooperative and collaborative working environment to gain 
their best performance.

{ii} Deci and Ryan's self-determination 
{1985} {HL only} 
Self-determination theory is the work of American 
psychologists Edward L. Deci (b.1942) and Richard M. Ryan 
(b.1953). They describe motivation as what moves or makes 
people to act. Self-determination theory (SDT) examines the 
fundamental and positive human tendency to grow (flourish). 
Deci and Ryan introduced their SDT theory in their book "Self-
Determination and Intrinsic Motivation in Human Behaviour" 
(1985), which outlines three core requirements that facilitate 
such growth: autonomy, competence and relatedness.

subject: Business Management
content:
Autonomy - This refers to the need or drive to have control 
over what a person does. When this need is satisfied, the 
person feels a sense of integrity and authenticity with their 
actions and decisions. When the need for autonomy is not 
met, the person feels frustrated, pressurized and pushed in 
an unwanted direction. 
Competence - This refers to the need or drive to feel 
confident and competent in doing a particular task or 
job role. It is about a sense of effectiveness, value and 
mastery. Competence can be achieved through providing 
and developing opportunities to use and extend people's 
skills and expertise. When this need is not met, the person 
experiences a sense of ineffectiveness, vulnerability and 
failure. 
Relatedness -
The refers to the need to interact, be 
connected to and experience caring for others. This need 
is met when people feel they have meaningful relationships 
and interactions with others, as well as feeling significant 
to others. If the need for relatedness is not met, people 
feel a sense of social alienation, exclusion and loneliness, 
all of which have a detrimental impact on motivation and 
productivity. 
Self-determination theory focuses on intrinsic motivation, 
which is intangible and internal to an individual, such as a sense 
of recognition, purpose and achievement

subject: Business Management

. Deci and Ryan's SDT 
concept suggests that these three needs or drivers of motivation 
are essential for intrinsic motivation because they help people 
to feel engaged, fulfilled and valued. The theory can help 
employers to gain a better understanding of how best to develop 
and engage their workforce as well as help individual employees

(financial and non-financial rewards). 
Typical inputs include expertise, experience, enthusiasm and 
effort. Inputs can be physical and intellectual. Outputs (also 
referred to as outcomes) typically include remuneration, 
recognition (praise), rank (status) and responsibilities. Outputs 
can be both tangible and intangible.

If inequities are not dealt with, absenteeism will increase 
and workers can become disruptive to the organization. In 
severe cases of inequities, workers might even take industrial 
action (see Chapter 13) or resign from their jobs. Therefore, 
an equitable balance in the ratio of inputs to outputs means 
workers should have greater satisfaction and motivation in their 
jobs, helping to ensure positive, productive and professional 
relationships at work. 
However, critics of equity theory point out that the concept 
of fairness is highly subjective. Two people with the same 
qualifications and skills, performing the same jobs for the same 
remuneration package might have very different perceptions of 
what is 'fair'. Some people are more sensitive to issues of equity 
than others; the theory ignores demographic, psychological 
and cultural factors that can affect perceptions of fairness. 
Furthermore, whilst workers can accept that senior staff are 
compensated more, there is a limit to the scales of equity so it 
can be highly demotivating if executive directors are excessively 
remunerated. Therefore, these issues and perceptions need to 
be managed effectively in business organizations

Equity (fairness) is not the same as equality (sameness).

The 
key difference between equity theory and 
expectancy theory is that: 
Equity theory suggests that people gain job 
satisfaction by comparing their effort (input) and 
reward (output) ratio with others. The employee is 
motivated ifs/he feels the input to output ratio is fair 
in line with others in the organization or society. 
Expectancy theory assumes that people behave in a 
certain way in exchange for rewards based on their 
conscious expectations. The employee is motivated 
if s/he intrinsically perceives that the reward is

abour turnover measures the percentage of the

For example, if twelve teachers left during the academic year in 
an 1B World School where 96 teachers are employed, the labour

The main reasons why people leave their jobs can be summed 
up by internationally best-selling author M.J. Yate, who used 
the acronym CLAMPS as the six acceptable reasons for labour 
turnover: Challenge, Location, Advancement, Money, Pride 
(or Prestige) and (Job) Security. If staff leave because they are 
demotivated or disgruntled, this raises concern for managers 
and employers. 
A low labour turnover rate suggests that the organization has 
recruited the right people for the job and that the existing 
employees are content and motivated at work. By contrast, a high 
labour turnover rate suggests that staff are incompetent or lack 
job satisfaction. It might also be due to better job opportunities 
and remuneration packages offered by other employers. In any 
case, a high labour turnover rate will clearly add to the costs 
of recruiting and training new staff in addition to the lost

Managers can use appraisals to provide constructive feedback

Appraisals can be a useful way of getting valuable feedback 
from employees to help the organization adapt and improve. 
Managers often aggregate the findings of appraisals to identify 
common strengths and areas in need of improvement. Thus, 
training and development needs can be better planned for the 
entire organization. 
Appraisals can be used as part of the process to determine 
levels of pay. This can be done by looking at the different tasks,

objectively reward more demanding roles with higher rates of

The HL syllabus specifies the following four types of appraisals: 
(i) formative, (ii) summative, (iii) 360-degree feedback and (iv) 
self-appraisal. 
{i} Formative appraisal 
Formative appraisal is the planned and ongoing process in 
which data and evidence are used to inform employees about 
what to do to improve their work practices. This type of appraisal 
enables managers and workers to engage in performance 
management conversations, encouraging employees to think 
about their own contributions to the organization. Formative 
assessment is commonly used in schools, such as teachers 
marking an end-of-topic test, grading it and adding written 
comments to inform students about how best to improve their 
performance. 
Formative appraisal is often used for appraising workers hired 
for a probation ( trial) period. For example, formative assessment 
is used to evaluate the competencies and performance of junior 
doctors, trainee teachers or novice supermarket workers during 
their apprenticeship or training period. The process helps the 
appraisee to modify his/her practices to improve their overall 
performance

subject: Business Management
content:
. Like most types of appraisals, the goals of 
formative appraisal include to: 
monitor the learning and performance of employees 
help employees identify their strengths and weaknesses 
(areas that need developing) 
help managers to recognise areas where staff are struggling 
so that any problems can be addressed promptly. 
For example, summative appraisals of teachers usually involve 
lesson observations carried out by senior managers, such as the 
school principal or one of the vice principals. They are similar 
to a summative report that students might get at school, often 
following a major assessment such as an end-of-year or mock 
examination. The feedback or review shows them what they 
have learned during the semester or the academic year, as well 
as targets for improvement. 
The goal of summative appraisal is to evaluate the performance 
or contribution of workers by comparing this with a pre-
determined standard or benchmark. Essentially, it is used 
to make a comprehensive and professional judgement of an 
employee's core competencies and to identify any specific areas 
in need of improvement. 
{iii) 360-degree feedback 
360-degree appraisal involves collecting evidence about the 
appraisee's job performance from a range of stakeholders who 
work with the employee

subordinates, line managers or other parties (such as suppliers 
or customers) who have direct contact with the employee. 
Opinions and feedback comments about the employee's 
performance are usually obtained by the use of questionnaires or 
interviews. The questions are focused on the core competencies 
of the appraisee, directly related to their job role. 
This method is a popular method of appraising managers, with 
the aim of providing useful and pragmatic feedback to improve 
managerial performance and effectiveness. However, such 
appraisals often rely heavily on opinions rather than factual 
evidence. Hence, this method is not suitable for all businesses.

Self-appraisal involves employees appraising themselves based 
on a set of pre-determined criteria. Appraisees are expected to 
be honest about their strengths and weaknesses. They also need 
to set realistic targets for improvement.

Financial rewards (A02) 
The following types of financial rewards: (i} salary, (ii} wages 
(time and piece rates}, (iii} commission, (iv} performance-related 
pay (PRP}. (v} profit-related pay, (vi} employee share ownership 
schemes and (vii} fringe payments. AO2

inancial rewards refer to the various methods that 
businesses use to motivate workers that involve some 
form of monetary payment. The main methods of 
financial rewards are considered below. 
{i} Salary 
Salaries are financial rewards set at a fixed annual rate but paid 
on a regular basis. For example, a person earning $36,000 per 
year is paid $3,000 per month or $1,500 fortnightly. Salaries can 
improve a firm's cash flow as workers are paid a fixed amount 
just once a month, usually directly into the employee's bank 
account. This is also safer and more convenient as there is no 
need to pay workers in cash. 
Salaried workers often have to work more than their contracted 
hours but are unlikely to be paid for this extra work as any 
overtime is usually considered to be part of the job (just ask 
your teachers!) By contrast, those earning wages might be paid 
in cash on a more regular basis ( usually weekly or even daily in 
some cases)

subject: Business Management

. 
Salaries are often used in professions where output or 
productivity is not easy to measure and where linking pay with 
speed can lead to lower quality standards, such as in the case of 
teachers, psychiatrists and healthcare professionals. However, 
salaries suffer from two key limitations:

To what extent might fixed salary payments limit

{ii} Wages {time and piece rates} 
Wages are the reward for labour services usually expressed 
as an hourly rate (time) or as a measurable quantity of output 
(piece rate). Wages based on time can be paid per hour, per 
day or per week. Low-skilled workers in manual jobs tend to 
be paid by hourly rates. The wage rate is likely to depend on the 
worker's experience and scope of responsibilities. 
In many countries, a national minimum wage is set by the 
government, so all employers must pay their workers no 
less than the stipulated rate. Wage earners are often paid an 
overtime rate for the hours they work over and above their 
contracted hours. It is common for the overtime rate to be paid 
at time and a half ( 50% extra pay per hour) or double pay ( 100% 
extra pay per hour) to compensate the employee for sacrificing 
more leisure time

There is little, if any, incentive to work harder since people 
are paid the same amount for their time. This can encourage 
slack or procrastination in the workplace. 
One way to deal with these problems is to introduce a formal 
appraisal system (see above). 
A key advantage of using wages is that it is a straightforward 
method which is easily understood by employees. However, the 
main disadvantage is that workers are not rewarded for their 
efforts but their time. This might encourage slack and poor 
productivity as well as hinder creativity and change. 
Piece rate is a payment system that can get around the problem 
of time-based wages by rewarding more productive workers. 
Piece rate, advocated by F.W Taylor, pays workers for each 
item that they produce or sell per time period. For instance, if 
a machinist in a clothing factory gets paid $1.50 per garment

The key advantage of piece rate is that employees have an 
incentive to work hard to maximise their earnings. However, 
there might be a trade-off between the quantity and quality of 
output, so there tends to be a need for supervision and quality 
control. Staff might also be demoralised due to the uncertain 
level of income from piece rate, often caused by factors beyond 
their own control (such as mechanical failure or extreme bad 
weather) which would reduce their output and productivity, 
thereby negatively impacting their earnings. 
Common mistake 
Students often use the terms 'salaries' and 'wages' 
interchangeably. This is inappropriate as salaries are 
a fixed cost whereas wages are a variable cost (see 
Chapter 16). Instead, it might be better for you to use 
the terms 'earnings' or 'remuneration~

In reality, the earnings of most employees are subject 
to personal income tax and other deductions. The total 
amount earned during a period of time is called the 
gross earnings. The government allows people to earn a 
certain amount of money (known as the tax allowance) 
before they pay income tax. The amount received after 
all deductions are paid is known as net earnings, i.e. the 
take-home pay. Whilst most jobs advertise the gross pay, 
it is the net pay that employees ultimately receive.

{iii) Commission 
Commission pays workers based on a proportion (percentage) 
of sales or output contributed by a worker. This contrasts with 
piece rate which is a fixed amount per unit made or sold. For 
example, real estate agents might get paid 1 % (the commission) 
of the value of each property that they sell. So, an agent who sells 
a $500,000 property would earn $5,000 in commission

payment system is commonly found in jobs where financial 
rewards act as an incentive to sell more. For example, insurance 
brokers receive a percentage of the premiums paid on policies 
that they have arranged. 
In reality, it is common for people on piece rate or commission 
to receive a basic salary. To some extent, this helps to meet their 
physiological needs so even if the person does not manage 
to sell anything, s/he will still be paid the basic amount of 
pay. However, for each item sold, the salesperson will earn 
commission thereby boosting his/her overall earnings.

A key advantage of PRP is that it creates incentives for people 
to work and perform better, especially if targets are clearly set. 
PRP is also seen as a fair system because hard work is rewarded 
(see Adams's equity theory above). Furthermore, PRP helps to 
develop a performance culture where people strive to achieve 
their targets in return for benefits such as opportunities for 
promotion or a financial bonus. 
However, PRP does suffer from several limitations such as the 
following points: 
Targets might be unrealistic or unachievable, so this can 
cause resentment and hinder job performance. 
The pressure imposed on workers to meet their targets 
can cause undue stress (especially if their pay is linked to 
achieving unrealistic performance targets)

Profit-related pay is used to strengthen employee loyalty and 
to foster team spirit because profits can only be achieved by 
combined team efforts rather than by an individual's input. 
As American football coach Vince Lombardi (1913 - 1970) 
said, "the achievements of an organization are the results of the 
combined effort of each individual." Hence, profit sharing should 
boost motivation and labour productivity as well as limit the 
possibility of potential conflict in the workplace. Another 
advantage is that it can help to break down a 'them and us' 
culture (see Chapter 11) as teams of managers and employees 
work together to achieve higher levels of profit. 
However, the proportion of profits paid to employees is often 
seen as too small to provide any real and sustainable incentive 
to work any harder. Walmart, the world's largest retailer, 
announced in 2007 that it was to bring back annual bonuses 
paying an average of$651 to its 1.3 million hourly-paid workers 
(but the pay-out equated to under $1.80 per day for each 
worker!) Also, individual efforts are not explicitly recognised

Important aspects of non-financial motivators are ignored 
under a PRP reward system. 
{v} Profit-related pay 
As a form of financial motivation, profit-related pay involves 
linking remuneration to the level of profits in the organization, 
i.e. the greater the profits, the higher the pay. Profit-related pay 
is usually paid as an annual bonus. For example, Southwest 
Airlines paid its workers an extra 11.3% in 2018 (the equivalent 
of 5 weeks' extra pay) as part of its $543 million profit-sharing 
to improve their own performance. By contrast, performance-
related pay (see above) is more flexible than profit-related pay 
as a reward system. In reality, profit sharing is often used to 
reward senior managers rather than for the entire workforce, 
especially as individuals lower down in the organizational 
hierarchy have no direct influence in changing the firm's overall 
level of profits

{vi} Employee share ownership schemes 
This payment system rewards workers, managers and directors 
by giving them shares in the company or by selling the shares at 
a discounted price. It is often used as an alternative to awarding 
a cash bonus or profit sharing. The motive for using employee 
share ownership schemes is that workers (who become 
shareholders of the company) will have a more direct interest 
in the well-being of the organization. Subsequently, employers 
gain from lower rates of staff absenteeism and labour turnover. 
In reality, share ownership schemes tend to work better for more 
senior managers and directors in the organization. The majority

{vi} Fringe payments 
Fringe payments (also known as financial perks) are the 
monetary benefits to employees in addition to their wages or 
salaries. Examples include health insurance, housing allowance, 
employer's contributions to employee retirement funds, staff 
discounts, subsidised meals, gym membership, paid holidays 
and paid sick leave. Fringe benefits vary from one business to 
another and often depend on an employee's position or rank in 
the organization. 
Figure 10.9 - Some businesses offer their employees free 
gym membership as a financial perk 
Key advantages of using fringe payments are that they boost 
staff morale and encourage employee loyalty. They can also help 
to meet the safety and esteem needs of employees (see Maslow's 
hierarchy of needs theory) and make workers feel more valued 
as the extra benefits help to enhance their overall remuneration. 
The main disadvantage ofusing fringe payments is the potentially 
high costs. For example, it is likely that all employees qualify to 
receive basic fringe benefits, such as annual paid leave (holiday 
pay), free uniforms, pension contributions and private medical 
cover

. In addition, senior managers might qualify for further 
fringe benefits, such as company cars, housing allowance and 
business-class air travel. These business expenses can be an 
enormous burden on a firm's cash flow position (see Chapter 
20).

Non-financial rewards {A02) 
The following types of non-financial rewards: (i) job enrichment, (ii) 
job rotation, (iii) job enlargement, (iv) empowerment, (v) purpose/ 
the opportunity to make a difference and (vi) teamwork. AO2 
© IBO, 2022

on-financial rewards are non-monetary factors 
that motivate people by offering psychological and 
intangible benefits, i.e. factors not directly linked to 
money. Most motivation theorists, including Deci and Ryan, 
McClelland, Maslow and Herzberg, advocate the use of non-
financial methods of motivation. Examples of non-financial 
rewards are explained below. 
{i} Job enrichment 
Herzberg emphasised that making a job more interesting or 
challenging is a crucial motivating factor. Job enrichment ( or 
vertical loading) gives workers more challenging jobs with 
more responsibilities. Hence, people have greater autonomy 
and authority in their work and have better opportunities to 
accomplish their jobs. It can also result in the psychological 
A key limitation of job enrichment is the added expenses of 
time and money needed to train and develop workers to fulfil 
these extra roles and responsibilities

subject: Business Management

. Another drawback is 
that job enlargement increases the workload of employees, 
which can cause anxiety, stress and hence lower productivity. 
Managers must also ensure that jobs are not too challenging 
or too complex for an employee who does not have the right 
skills set because this would lead to disastrous outcomes and 
can destroy the confidence and morale of the worker. 
{ii} Job rotation 
Job rotation is a type of non-financial reward that involves 
workers performing different tasks at the same level of 
complexity in a systematic way. This means that employees 
perform a number of different tasks in a particular order or 
growth of employees, so they become more committed to their 
sequence. For example, supermarket employees might work at 
work. Furthermore, the ability to do a variety of tasks means that 
the checkouts as cashiers one day, then rotate to work in other 
workers have a better sense of engagement and achievement.

Figure 10.10 - Job rotation is commonly found in large

The intention of job rotation is to provide more variety to avoid 
the problems of over-specialization (such as boredom caused by 
performing the same tasks repetitively). Job rotation also makes 
it easier for people to cover for absent colleagues as they become 
more familiar with a range of job roles. However, multiskilling 
requires greater costs of training and can be regarded by some 
employees as simply adding to their workload without any real 
career development opportunities. 
(iii) Job enlargement 
Job enlargement (also known as horizontal loading) refers 
to broadening the number of tasks that an employee performs, 
although the nature of the job itself remains essentially 
unchanged. For example, an administrative worker might 
spend most of the day looking after the reception area, dealing 
with customer enquiries, but also spend some time on data 
input, photocopying documents, filing and other clerical tasks. 
One purpose (advantage) of job enlargement is that it reduces 
the monotony or repetitiveness of tasks that can cause boredom 
and demotivation. Job enlargement can make work more 
interesting as it involves employees having a wider range of 
tasks

subject: Business Management
content:
. However, some employees might view this as a way to 
get them to do more work for the same amount of pay, thus 
leading to demoralised and demotivated workers. In addition, 
any benefits of job enlargement are likely to diminish after a 
period of time if the roles become mundane (unexciting and 
unchallenging). Finally, the continual enlargement of a job 
over time can lead to unmanageable workloads for staff, thus 
causing demotivation. 
2.4 Motivation and demotivation 
Exam tip! 
Be sure you know the difference between job enrichment 
and job enlargement. Job enrichment (vertical expansion 
of roles) is essentially dependent on job enlargement 
(horizontal expansion of job roles) whereas job 
enlargement can take place without job enrichment. Job 
enrichment is most helpful for employees who want to 
advance in their professional careers. 
(iv) Empowerment 
Empowerment is about developing the potential of workers 
or teams to achieve the best they can. It involves granting 
workers the authority to be in charge of their own jobs and 
to execute their own ideas to solve business problems. Hence, 
workers have some autonomy in decision-making so can 
decide for themselves the best way to deal with a task or issue

subject: Business Management
content:
. 
Empowerment can boost motivation as workers can take 
initiative and have a say in how things are done. Thus, they 
have a greater sense of pride in their work. For instance, in the 
education profession, the principal of a school usually allows 
subject teachers to plan and deliver lessons in a way that they 
see most appropriate for their students. 
Empowerment requires giving workers the necessary authority, 
skills, resources and opportunities to achieve individual 
and organizational objectives (see Chapter 3). As Chinese 
philosopher Confucius (551 BC - 479 BC) said, "J hear and I 
forget. I see and I remember. I do and I understand:' 
Empowerment can be achieved through various methods, 
including: 
Delegation - This occurs when managers pass on authority 
to their subordinates, allowing them to take charge of 
a particular job role and to gain recognition for his/her 
accomplishments. Delegation works best when subordinates 
have the competence (ability) and desire (willingness) to 
take on additional responsibilities. Managers must also 
ensure that staff are given sufficient time and resources to 
accomplish the delegated tasks. Successful delegation can 
therefore boost motivation and help employees to gain 
invaluable experiences to progress in their careers

.

have opportunities to participate in decision-making, 
so they feel engaged and empowered, such as by using

the business provides them with authentic training and 
development opportunities. This can also help workers to 
progress in their professional careers. 
However, empowerment must be used appropriately. Delegating 
tasks to empower staff can only be successful if the workers 
have adequate skills and have received the necessary training 
to independently deal with given tasks and roles. Managers 
are still held responsible for the tasks or projects they delegate, 
so inappropriate use of empowerment can lead to expensive 
mistakes being made

. 
Exam tip! 
Delegation can empower a worker by giving to him/her 
the authority to take charge of a particular task or project. 
However, the responsibility of success or failure ultimately 
stays with the manager. In other words, authority can be 
delegated but responsibility cannot. 
{iv) Purpose {the opportunity to make a 
difference) 
Whilst some employees are driven by self-interest, others are 
motivated by using their work to help others thereby making a 
difference to the world we live in. Such employees are altruistic 
(selfless) and see the purpose of work being to make a positive 
change in other people's lives. Doctors, nurses, social care 
workers, firefighters and teachers are examples. History has 
shown that during times of crises, people cooperate to help 
each other. 
Very importantly, purpose is about the role or job itself 
rather than acts of altruism such as donating money to an 
external charity (which only generates perceived impacts on 
170 
beneficiaries). The motivation to make a difference occurs when 
people have the opportunity to build ongoing relationships 
with the beneficiaries. This is apparent with charity and social 
care workers who are fully committed to their work in making 
a difference to others

McKinsey & Company, the American global management 
consultancy firm, has shown through numerous studies that 
people with satisfactory salaries need more than financial 
rewards to sustain motivation. The studies showed some non-
financial rewards are more effective than additional pay. The 
opportunity to help others or to make a difference to society 
can be motivational and give workers a real sense of purpose. 
Financial rewards such as bonuses or employee share options 
generate short-term gains in motivation but can have negative 
unintended consequences due to the expectation that these 
rewards become the norm. Philanthropy and alumni donations 
are common examples of how all employees can make a 
difference to others.

{v} Teamwork 
"A boat doesn't go forward if each one is rowing their own way." 
- Swahili Proverb 
Teamwork occurs when employees work with fellow colleagues. 
An example is teams that work together in their respective 
functional areas (see Chapter 1), such as departmental teams 
in finance, marketing and operations management. Another 
example is quality circles (see Chapter 37) which involves team 
members meeting regularly to discuss solutions to problems 
regarding quality within the production process. 
Teamwork can help to meet the social needs of employees 
by building a sense of belonging. It can also help to reduce 
boredom (of working alone). Hence, this type of non-financial 
motivation can help to reduce absenteeism and labour turnover 
whilst boosting morale and productivity. It can also lead to 
greater flexibility and multi-skilling because employees learn 
from working with other team members. Hence, workers 
can cover for one another during times of absences without 
delaying the production process or reducing the quality of the 
service being delivered.

Maslow's hierarchy of needs). When each employee's 
self-worth is boosted through motivation, the business 
is more likely to flourish.

Table 10.7 -The advantages and disadvantages of induction training 
Advantages of induction training 
Establishes clear expectations and good working habits from 
the start. 
Helps new recruits to understand the corporate culture of the 
organization. 
By settling in quicker, new recruits can contribute to the 
organization more promptly. 
Morale is boosted as new staff feel welcome and are more 
confident and competent in their job roles. 
(ii) On the job training 
On the job training refers to training carried out whilst at 
the workplace. For example, the training can be delivered by 
a manager, supervisor or other specialist. The trainees learn 
from the skilled colleague who delivers the training at the place 
of work. Essentially, this type of training involves 'learning by 
doing'. As Chinese philosopher Confucius said, "I hear and I 
forget. I see and I remember. I do and I understand". 
Common examples of on the job training include: 
Demonstration - This involves an employee observing and 
learning about a specific task or process being carried out 
from an experienced member of staff. The trainer then 
supports the trainees who are given the opportunity to 
attempt these tasks and processes themselves

subject: Business Management
content:
. 
Shadowing - This refers to junior staff or new recruits 
observing and learning from more experienced and 
senior employees. This approach is commonly used for 
apprenticeship and internship schemes. The trainer allows 
the trainee to have a try at different aspects of the task, 
as well as provides suggestions and feedback to help the 
trainee to make progress. 
Disadvantages of induction training 
Planning, delivering and overseeing an induction course can be 
time consuming. 
Trainers cannot carry out their other duties as they are involved 
in providing induction. 
Information overload is counter-productive for new staff who 
have to absorb so much information. 
The length of induction programmes can be very long, 
especially in large and disparate organizations. 
Job rotation - This involves employees doing different 
jobs and learning the processes and procedures associated 
with these roles. This type of on the job training focuses 
on knowledge specific to the job and helps to promote 
cohesiveness in the workforce. 
Practice simulations - These are training opportunities 
that put employees in certain job-like scenarios. These 
simulations replicate the situations the employee is likely 
to face at work

of hours in practice simulations each year to ensure they 
are appropriately upskilled and able to cope with every 
foreseeable scenario.

Motivation and the key concepts 
One of the earliest recorded English proverbs is that "You can 
take a horse to water, but you cannot force it to drink the water." 
This is because the horse will only drink if it is thirsty. Likewise, 
people will only perform their jobs well if they are motivated to 
do so. Furthermore, sustaining motivation in the workplace is 
hugely challenging. Productivity is dependent on an employee's 
level of ability and sustained motivation. The failure to motivate 
workers can lead to a range of problems, such as higher 
absenteeism, increased labour turnover, poor customer service 
and lower quality output. By contrast, a culture that fosters 
motivation leads to better labour retention and its associated 
benefits (see Box 10.6). 
Box 10.6 - Benefits of higher staff retention 
Retention is the opposite of labour turnover, i.e. it 
measures the proportion of the workforce that choose to 
remain working at the organization, rather than leave it. 
The benefits of staff retention include: 
Lower costs of recruitment, selection, induction and 
training of new staff. 
Improved corporate image, thereby making it easier to 
recruit new staff. 
Skills, knowledge and expertise are kept within the firm

subject: Business Management
content:
. 
A strong and unified corporate culture is established. 
Improved competitiveness and profitability, due to the 
above benefits. 
However, there is no general strategy that best motivates all 
employees. This is largely because each and every individual 
worker is different. People are likely to be motivated by a 
combination of both intrinsic and extrinsic factors. Intrinsic 
motivation occurs when people engage in an activity out of their 
own desire, such as the enjoyment of pursuing a hobby or an 
interest because the person finds it to be challenging, stimulating 
or fun. Thus, intrinsically motivated students would want to 
master a subject rather than rote learn the subject simply to get 
good examination grades. Intrinsic motivation can also occur 
due to altruistic reasons, i.e. there is a sense of commitment 
to others. In many Asian cultures, intrinsic motivation occurs 
due to family reasons. For example, students seek to work hard 
2.4 Motivation and demotivation 
partly due to family pressures and partly to avoid letting down 
their parents. 
By contrast, extrinsic motivation occurs when people participate 
in an activity because of the benefits and rewards associated with 
doing so

subject: Business Management
content:
. These incentives might be tangible (such as wages, 
salaries and bonuses) or intangible (such as recognition and 
praise). Extrinsic motivation can also arise from organizational 
cultures that use pressure and threats, that is, workers engage in 
an activity to avoid punishments irrespective of whether this is 
deemed to be unethical. Some managers do not see any value 
in using non-financial motivators for workers who do not want 
responsibility or lack skills and ambition. 
Change also has a major impact on motivation, productivity 
and job satisfaction. In reality, motivating the workforce is an 
extremely complex task because there are so many different 
factors to consider, each of which is subject to change. What 
motivates one person does not automatically motivate another. 
For example, the threat of redundancies for some people creates 
a sense of fear which might drive them to work harder in an 
attempt to secure their jobs. For others, the insecurity does 
not motivate but acts as a dissatisfier (refer to Maslow's safety 
needs). 
Managers must therefore weigh up the costs of using various 
methods of motivation (such as profit-related pay) with the 
expected benefits (such as higher productivity)

.

the complex nature of strategically managing people

ever truly know what motivates different employees?

to (i) when organizations grow and merge and (ii) when leadership

I 
n reality, although one type of cultural dimension might 
dominate in a particular organization, country or region, 
there may be some groups that conform to other cultures 
or subcultures. These groups may have different opinions, 
values, beliefs and interests to the perceived cultural norms of 
the organization. This discrepancy among subgroups can cause 
a culture gap - the difference between the desired culture of a 
business and the culture(s) that actually exists. 
Figure 11.3 - Values are the beliefs and moral stance of an 
organization 
Culture clashes exist when there is conflict or incompatibility 
between two or more cultures within an organization. This 
can exist when firms grow organically, merge with other 
organizations, expands overseas or when there is a change in 
leadership. 
Reasons for organizational cultural clashes 
Growth of firms - The internal growth of firms is likely 
to lead to a more formal and hierarchical organizational 
structure (see Chapter 8)

subject: Business Management
content:
. This can result in organizations 
becoming more bureaucratic and power orientated in 
order to maintain control and coordination. In other 
organizations, an adaptive culture acts as the source of 
growth and evolution, rather than being the result of 
growth. Adaptive cultures exist in organizations that are 
responsive and receptive to change. Such organizations 
tend to be highly creative and embrace change. Culture 
clashes often also occur when businesses expand into 
overseas markets, especially if managers and workers are 
ignorant of differences in national cultures, for example. 
Case study 11.2 - McDonald's Drive Thru 
In 2005, McDonald's introduced the Drive-thru concept 
to China. However, this American cultural export was so 
abstract to Chinese drivers at the time that they actually 
bought food at the Drive-thru, parked their vehicles in 
the car park and then proceeded to eat their meals inside 
the McDonald's restaurants! 
Mergers and acquisitions (M&As) - Organizational 
cultures can clash or change when there is external growth, 
such as a merger with another company or an acquisition 
of another organization. In theory, M&As should help the 
organizations involved to gain from economies of scale 
(see Chapter 6)

subject: Business Management
content:
. However, M&As can fail due to culture 
clashes. Even if the merger goes ahead, the culture of the 
more dominant company tends to prevail or a new hybrid 
culture develops. In reality, those who cannot adapt to the 
new culture are likely to leave the organization. 
Change in leadership - Leaders can have a huge influence 
on organizational culture (see Box 11.1). The qualities of 
effective leaders, such as their vision and interpersonal 
skills, influence the values and behaviours of the workforce 
thereby shaping the desired corporate culture. Leadership 
styles (see Chapter 10) are a key factor affecting corporate 
culture. Hence, a change in leadership can easily result in a 
change in the organizational culture. For example, consider 
how your school principal shapes the culture of the school 
and what might happen if s/he resigned. Leaders drive the 
strategic direction of the organization, so a change in the 
leadership team can result in culture clashes (see Question 
11.2).

Box 11.1 MOVER Leadership 
A challenge for leaders is to influence people within their 
organizations to follow a shared vision and corporate 
culture. Strategies to achieve this include being a MOVER: 
• Mentor - Leaders act as mentors (see Chapter 7) by 
sharing their knowledge and expertise and supporting 
their teams to mould a healthy organizational culture. 
This also helps to build trust within the organization. 
• Outreach - Communicating the vision and desired 
culture to all members of the organization, so everyone 
moves in the same direction and holds the same values. 
• Vision - Without knowing where the business wants to 
be, it is impossible and pointless trying to guide and 
motivate staff. 
• Engaging - The desired corporate culture must engage 
and excite the workforce, perhaps by the leader 
nurturing a sense of self-worth and commitment to 
the goals of the organization. Empowering others (see 
Chapter 10) also means a greater number of individuals 
can help to shape the desired organizational culture. 
• Role modelling - As Mahatma Gandhi (1869 - 1948) 
said, "You must be the change you wish to see in the 
world'; i

Organizational culture and the key 
concepts 
Understanding organizational culture is important for the 
effective management of any organization. Cultural intelligence 
or cultural quotient (CQ), is the ability of an individual to 
blend into occupational, corporate and national cultures. CQ 
is an indicator of a worker's ability to cope with change. The 
term was coined by Professor Christopher Earley and Professor 
Elaine Mosakowski in the Harvard Business Review (2004). 
Cultural quotient is important, especially during times of 
change, as it measures the ability of people to understand and 
adjust to unfamiliar situations such as a hostile takeover (see 
Unit 1.6) or a crisis (see Unit 5.7). 
Organizational cultures change, develop and strengthen over 
time. Beliefs, norms, attitudes and values are more likely to be 
shared within the organization if they are given the time to do 
so. This makes any attempt to change the organizational culture 
188 
a more challenging task. Nevertheless, as markets become more 
competitive and globalized organizations are forced into being 
more adaptive to change, creativity and innovation. In addition, 
political, economic, social, technological and legal changes (see 
Chapter 46) may require organizational cultures to adapt and 
embrace changes in the external business environment

subject: Business Management
content:
. For 
example, the outbreak of the COVID-19 pandemic caused 
huge changes to working practices as many people switched to 
working from home and relied on Internet technologies and 
videoconferencing platforms such as Zoom, Skype, Google 
Meet and Microsoft Teams to conduct their work.

Theory of Knowledge {TOK) 
Have Internet technologies disrupted indigenous 
cultures? 
Organizational culture impacts on the attitude of workers 
towards change. If employees are not interested in pursuing 
change, this could harm the business's ability to achieve its 
goals and to operate in a sustainable manner. A weak, negative 
and undesirable culture can lead to increased absenteeism, 
lateness and conflict, thereby intensifying costs for the business. 
By contrast, a strong culture of acceptance to change and 
embracing creative solutions to solving business issues will 
support an organization in responding to the changing needs of 
the market. Cultural harmony within an organization can only 
come about if all staff understand and share the same values. 
Without a shared vision, culture gaps and conflict can cause 
major problems for the organization. 
Finally, it is important to recognize that it might not be possible 
or realistic to have just one culture within an organization, 
especially in large multinational companies where sub-cultures 
may exist. Today, societies face greater influences from other 
cultures, especially with the cultural diversity of people in many 
organizations

Formal and informal communication 
Communication can also be classified as formal or informal. 
Formal communication refers to all official channels of 
communication. It is directly related to work matters, such as 
a discussion about who is the best candidate for a job vacancy 
or simply instructions or information being passed down from 
managers to their subordinates. Formal communication can be 
further categorized as open channels (used when information 
is not confidential and can be shared by anyone in an official 
capacity) or restricted channels ( used when formal information 
is confidential and is directed only at those who need to know). 
The subsequent section in this chapter covers the various 
methods of formal communication for an organization. 
Informal communication ( or grapevine communication) 
refers to all unofficial, natural and unstructured communication 
channels that exist among informal groups within an 
organization, such as people from different departments 
talking about work- and non-work-related matters during 
their lunch break together. Such communications are free 
from organizational formalities. Informal groups tend to 
occur naturally because members share common interests, 
not because they are formally part of the organization

spoken, written or even conveyed through body language and 
physical gestures. Other examples of informal communication

the same division or functional areas. 
Casual conversations with work colleagues, be it the 
canteen, a corridor or at a social event after work. Informal 
conversations are an essential part of all businesses. 
Instant messaging platforms such as WhatsApp, WeChat 
and Facebook Messenger and other apps such as Instagram. 
These informal channels of communication are particularly 
popular with younger employees.

informal communication can be damaging to a business 
especially if the wrong message gets leaked out to external

However, other managers see informal communications in 
a more positive manner, suggesting that there are numerous 
benefits: 
Informal communication can foster a sense of belonging 
in the workplace. People from different departments can 
talk about non-work issues over lunch breaks or at social 
gatherings, for example. This can help to meet their social 
needs at work, as well as improving morale and motivation 
in the workplace (see Chapter 10). 
It can also foster a sense of security and mutual support. 
People can talk to colleagues who are regarded as friends in 
addition to being a work colleague perhaps to get messages 
clarified or to deal with any concerns or anxieties that they 
might have. 
The pooling of ideas of people across the organization can 
help to generate solutions that might not have emerged 
through more formal communication channels. People are 
also more likely to be open and creative during informal 
discussions

improved professional relationships, create a greater sense 
of belonging and help to distribute information more easily 
and effectively. It can also help management to receive 
more honest feedback and suggestions.

Methods of formal communication for an organization include: 
(i) verbal, (ii) written, (iii) visual and (iv) non-visual channels 
of communication. 
(i) Verbal communication 
Verbal communication (or oral communication) refers 
to communication via the use of spoken words

. It involves 
people talking and listening to one another, such as meetings, 
interviews and appraisals. It is quick because the sender and 
receiver are usually in direct contact with each other. Oral 
communication allows questions to be asked and for feedback 
and clarification to be given. However, whether a message 
is communicated well verbally depends on the skills of the 
speaker, such as the use of jargon or the tone of voice. 
Examples of verbal communication include: 
Giving instructions or information, such as directors 
announcing and explaining a major change in the 
organization. 
Discussing problems in formal business meetings. Formal

meeting. Each agenda item will be discussed in turn with 
time scheduled for 'any other business' (AOB) at the end. A 
record of the meeting ( called the minutes) is documented 
and shared with relevant people, which can be used for 
future reference. 
Job interviews for the recruitment and selection of staff. 
Job appraisals (see Chapter 7) as part of the organization's 
performance review process. 
Verbal presentations, such as at staff meetings, sales pitches, 
product launch events and at press conferences

b} Memorandum 
A memorandum (or memo for short) is a business note from 
one person to another. It can be a formal typed note or simply 
a hand-written message. Memos are used for internal purposes, 
such as when managers wish to call a meeting (see Figure 12.6), 
to send a reminder or when people want to pass on a quick 
message.

A memorandum can be very quick to produce. Also, as the 
message is short and specific, it should be easy to understand. 
They are not usually intended or useful for long messages or for 
passing on complicated information. 
c} Reports 
Reports are a formal method of written communication 
whereby information about something that has been researched

format and will tend to have: 
A title (cover) page with information such as the name of 
the author of the report, the audience it is targeted at and

An executive summary of what the report is about and the 
purpose of the research or investigation. 
A contents page with page numbering. 
An introduction to the report. 
Section headings to separate parts of the report, especially 
if it is a long document. 
Conclusions and recommendations, where appropriate. 
A bibliography listing all sources of reference. 
An appendix with supplementary evidence, such as 
quantitative research data. 
Business reports are prepared in detail for a specified audience 
and this makes communication direct and easier to understand. 
However, it can take a long time to investigate and produce 
written reports, by which time any findings or recommendations 
made might be outdated. 
d} Notices 
N otices are used when a message needs to reach a range of 
people, perhaps by postings on staff notice boards or on a 
company website as well as notices for customers. Notices 
can be formal, such as highlighting training opportunities 
or fire evacuation procedures. They can also be informal to 
the business, such as sponsorship notices for a charity event. 
Notices are often communicated on notice boards ( or display 
boards) in the workplace. 
Notices are useful for passing on messages so that everyone can

Executives and directors do not have the time to read so many

f) Abstract 
An abstract (also known as a precis or synopsis) is written 
as a condensed (shortened) version of a report without losing 
the original message of the report. It differs slightly from an 
executive summary in that an abstract does not directly provide 
any recommendations to aid decision making

subject: Business Management

. An executive 
summary not only provides a summary of a report, but also 
the main findings and recommendations. In essence, a manager 
could do without reading the entire report if there is a succinct 
executive summary. This is not possible with an abstract alone 
as it does not include an evaluation of the main report. Abstracts 
also tend to be shorter than executive summaries. 
g) Research proposals 
A research proposal is a management planning document. It 
sets out the key issue(s) to be investigated. The research proposal 
may contain details of primary and secondary methods of 
research, an action plan with key dates and identification of 
any foreseeable problems (anticipated difficulties) likely to be 
encountered during the investigation process. 
A major disadvantage of all written forms of communication 
is the issue of storage. Despite the use of ICT and cloud 
computing, businesses today use more paper than ever before. 
Managers need to be disciplined in this aspect - how long should 
businesses hold written records for? In addition, many types of 
written communication are slow and if the receiver does not 
understand the written message, there will be further delays

(iv) Non-verbal communication 
Except for oral communication, all forms of communication 
can come under the category of non-verbal communication. 
This refers to any form of communication other than oral 
communication, such as electronic systems (such as email), 
written methods (such as letters) and visual stimulus (such 
as body language). Examples of !CT-based non-verbal 
communication methods are outlined below. 
a) Electronic mail (e-mail) 
Electronic mail refers to the process of using computer wide 
area networks (WAN) as a mailing system. Data is electronically 
transmitted from one computer to another. It is a very fast 
method of communication because all the data (text, graphs, 
charts and images) are already in electronic form. Data can also 
be transmitted to many different recipients at the same time, all 
across the world

c} Mobile devices 
The traditional telephone is still immensely popular as a means 
of communication in the business world. However, smartphones 
and other mobile devices, such as tablet computers, have taken 
over in terms of popularity and ownership. The top four mobile 
phone producers surpassed one billion units for the first time in 
2007. By 2021, there were 5.22 billion smartphone users around 
the world - around 66% of the world's population. The average 
person in Finland owns more than 2 mobile phones, whilst 
people in Japan replace their smartphones every nine months, 
on average. 
Mobile devices are used by managers and employees who 
are increasingly 'on the go'. such as real estate agents, sales 
representatives, insurance brokers and teleworkers (see 
Chapter 7). Technological progress, such as improved camera 
technologies and improve Wi-Fi coverage, has also further 
popularised the use of mobile devices as a form of information 
communication technology. As with videoconferences, the use 
of mobile devices facilitates both verbal and non-verbal forms

of communication (such as instant text messages sent using 
smartphone apps). 
In summary, electronic methods of communications have a 
growing importance in the global business world. ICT has 
allowed for faster yet cheaper communications over long 
distances. 
However, this can mean the need to purchase 
and maintain expensive software and computer hardware. 
Whilst email can be cost effective, the use of smartphones for 
international calls can still be rather expensive. Businesses that 
rely heavily on ICT find that things tend to come to a standstill 
when computers and electronic equipment fail, perhaps due to 
technical problems or power outages. 
Theory of Knowledge {TOK) 
Management guru Peter F. Drucker said that "the most 
important thing in communication is to hear what isn't 
being said''. How can we know what we do not hear? 
In reality, businesses will use a mix of communication methods 
to fit their individual requirements and different situations. 
The type of communication method chosen depends upon a 
combination of the factors outlined below. 
Personal preferences - Some people may prefer to hold 
conversations with others about problems or issues,

. 
Organizational structures - A tall organizational structure, 
with many hierarchical structures, (see Chapter 8) requires 
more formal and sophisticated methods of communication. 
Security issues and concerns - For example, hard copies 
of important documents are often kept in case computer 
files get damaged or corrupted by a virus or hardware 
malfunction. 
Skills and training of the users - Many schools, for example, 
use a range of ICT to enhance teaching and learning, 
including remote and distance learning. However, unless 
the teachers have received proper training to use the 
equipment and software, such investments can be a waste 
of money as they are not fully utilised. 
Ease of use - Some people may prefer to use a sketch as 
part of their presentation rather than using technical 
software such as PowerPoint or Prezi. Sending out flyers 
to customers might be easier for many people rather than 
setting up their own website to convey the same marketing 
message. 
Size of business - Large firms with multiple locations might 
rely on emails to serve their communication needs, whereas 
a small business might prefer to mainly use verbal methods 
of communication.

customers, colleagues and suppliers. Not listening to customers can be a costly mistake - dissatisfied customers mean a 
loss of sales and less loyalty to the organization. Negative messages can be spread by customers very quickly via social 
media platforms. Most experts feel that effective communications management involves listening to what employees 
have to say and having genuine consideration for their needs. 
In addition to listening skills, good communicators also show positive body language, such as a warm smile and making 
eye contact when speaking to someone. Research has shown communication is 7% dependent on spoken words, 38% on 
the tone of the voice, whilst the remaining 55% is on non-verbal signals.

Employees are usually represented by a trade union (or labour 
union) in their approach to conflict in the workplace. This is an 
organization whose members unite to protect their employment 
rights and welfare. Employee representatives coordinate 
industrial action in cases of industrial disputes. Industrial 
action refers to the activities taken by disgruntled employees 
due to disputes about pay and/or terms and conditions of 
work. It is a result of poor employer-employee relationships or 
conflict at work. 
The primary role of labour unions is to protect the interests of 
their members, such as: 
• 
Increased pay (or the prevention of pay cuts as is often the 
case). 
Improved remuneration, such as fringe benefits and paid 
holidays. 
• 
Better working terms and conditions, such as hours of 
work and rest breaks. 
• 
Opportunities for training, development and career 
progression. 
Better-quality staff facilities, such as an improved staff 
canteen or working spaces

An individual is unlikely to have much bargaining power 
compared with a union of workers due to the strength in 
numbers. From an employer's perspective, it is also cheaper and

Members of a trade union pay an annual fee to cover the costs 
of running the labour union. Examples of the main issues that

Membership fees also contribute towards the costs of legal

• Craft unions - These were the original labour unions

Employees and trade union members use the following 
approaches to conflict resolution in the workplace: (i) collective 
bargaining, (ii) work-to-rule and (iii) strike action. 
{i} Collective bargaining 
Collective bargaining is the negotiation process whereby trade 
union representatives and employer representatives discuss 
issues with the intention of reaching a mutually acceptable 
agreement. Individual employees are unlikely to be in a good 
position to negotiate with their employers. However, this 
weakness is removed when the workforce is united, via trade 
union representation. Subsequently, senior managers are more 
pressurised to listen to the views of the workers. A united 
workforce benefits from an increase in its collective bargaining 
(negotiation) power during the conflict resolution process. 
{ii} Work-to-rule 
Work-to-rule occurs when employees do the absolute minimum 
required according to the rules set by the employer. Workers 
adhere precisely to all rules and regulations in their deliberate 
attempts to delay production and to reduce productivity

subject: Business Management
content:
. Any 
goodwill from staff is withdrawn; workers do no more than 
they absolutely need to. For example, office staff may refuse to 
answer telephone calls during lunch breaks or choose to leave 
work as soon as their scheduled shift finishes. Such industrial 
action is considered less disruptive than strike action as workers 
are simply just obeying rules and regulations in a meticulous 
210 
manner. Hence, employers find it more difficult to discipline 
staff who work to rule. 
A variation of work-to-rule is go-slows. This involves employees 
working at the minimum pace allowable in their employment 
contract as they adhere to every organization rule and policy. 
This reduces productivity yet employers find it difficult to 
discipline staff who work at a slow but contractually acceptable 
pace, following internal rules and procedures. Overtime work 
is avoided (as there is no rule or requirement to do so) and 
any sense of urgency ceases as employees seek to minimise 
the speed of their work. Go-slows can be highly effective for 
workers when businesses face imminent deadlines or during 
periods of high seasonal demand because their operations 
become extremely disrupted. 
Theory of Knowledge (TOK} 
The EU's Working Time Directive (2003) states that all 
workers in the European Union must not be required 
to work more than 48 hours in a week, with a minimum 
rest period of at least 11 hours a day

subject: Business Management
