The effectiveness of crisis management is dependent on several 
factors, namely: (i) transparency, (ii) communication, (iii) 
speed and (iv) control in dealing with a crisis situation

subject: Business Management
content:
. 
(i) Transparency 
Transparency refers to being open and honest with all 
stakeholders during a crisis. It is about disclosing the truth, such 
as the scale or severity of the crisis. Most crisis management 
experts believe that it is best to be transparent (open and 
honest) during a time of crisis. Three examples from different 
decades are outlined below. 
In 1990, authorities in the USA found traces of benzene 
in Perrier bottled mineral water. Perrier, owned by Nestle, 
tried to hide the truth from the general public, but this only 
served to damage its corporate image. The mass media saw 
Perrier putting profits before the interest of people and this 
led to the recall of 160 million bottles of its natural mineral 
water. 
Sanlu Group was given a bankruptcy order from the 
Chinese government in 2008 for its involvement and 
attempted cover up in an adulterated baby milk powder 
scandal. Sanlu Group was found guilty of contaminating 
its product with traces of melamine, which caused kidney 
stones and other complications in almost 300,000 infants. 
In 2015, the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) 
found that Volkswagen, Europe's largest carmaker, had 
deliberately programmed its diesel engines to cheat 
laboratory emissions tests, which were about 40 times 
higher than what is allowed in the USA

subject: Business Management
content:
. The scandal 
resulted in its share price plummeting and the CEO 
resigning. The German company had to spend $18.32bn 
to rectify the emissions issue and faced a criminal fine of 
$2.8bn in 2017.

5.7 Crisis management and contingency planning (HL only) 
The lesson to be learnt is that in times of such crises, acting in 
a socially irresponsible way with a lack of transparency is far 
more likely to cause long-term damage to the organization than 
if it had acted responsibly and taken the necessary corrective 
measures from the outset. 
{ii} Communication 
Communication refers to the transmission of information, by 
informing internal and external stakeholders to help them to 
know about and understand the issue. Effective communication 
with all key stakeholder groups is critical in a crisis situation, 
such as contacting the emergency services and insurers. 
Effective crisis management also requires leaders to develop 
a crisis communications plan, including an understanding of 
how the news media works. In the event of a crisis, leaders need 
to get a press release out immediately to contain the situation. 
They need to work with the media and attempt to get the press 
on their side. 
Figure 41.4 - Effective communication is vital in a crisis 
situation 
With the use of Internet technologies and social media 
platforms, it is relatively easy to communicate via the 
organization's website

subject: Business Management
content:
. This was the method used by Apple 
when announcing the death of Steve Jobs in 2011, the company's 
CEO at the time. Effective communications help to reassure 
employees, customers, suppliers, shareholders, investors and 
other stakeholder groups. 
Common mistake 
Too often, students write about major crises, assuming 
that crises have to occur on a national or international 
scale. However, crises can occur on a small scale, 
affecting a single organization. Examples include an 
unexpected power cut, machinery breakdown or the 
sudden illness of the CEO or owner of the business. 
(iii) Speed 
Speed refers to making prompt decisions and taking swift 
actions in order to return the business to normal operations 
as soon as possible. In a crisis situation, the speed of response 
is critical to the effectiveness of crisis management. This is 
comparable to a person who has had a major accident and 
needs immediate medical attention; if the critically injured 
person is treated straight away, the chances of survival increase 
significantly. The same principle applies to corporate crisis 
management situations. The speed of response to the crisis 
influences the chances of containing or reducing the damages 
caused

subject: Business Management
content:
. This is far more likely to happen if managers have an 
effective contingency plan and can act swiftly in emergency 
situations. 
In 2022, Northern Powergrid, a British energy company owned 
by Berkshire Hathaway Energy, made a huge clerical error 
by sending out 74 cheques each for the sum of around £2.3 
trillion ($3.26 trillion) to compensate customers affected by up 
to 13 days of power outages in November 2021. The company 
had noticed the error in time to prevent any cheques from 
being cashed and quickly communicated the error to its key 
stakeholder groups, with a fitting apology. 
{iv) Control 
Control refers to the use of a crisis management ( or critical 
incident) team to handle an emergency situation and to ensure 
there is leadership and governance. A major crisis truly tests 
the performance and competence of the leadership team 
within an organization. Leaders need to be able to control the 
crisis situation. This entails many skills, including the ability 
to work under extreme pressures, to communicate with all 
key stakeholders (including the ability to manage the news 
media) and to make quick and effective decisions. A crisis will 
require leaders to have instant access to cash funds to control 
the situation and to continue business as usual ( or as much 
as possible)

The nuclear disaster caused substantial amounts of radioactive

The impact of contingency 
planning 
The impact of contingency planning for a given organization or 
situation in terms of: (i) cost, (ii) time, (iii) risks and (iv) safety. A03 
© IBO, 2022 
The impacts of contingency planning, be they advantages or 
disadvantages, for a given business organization or situation 
can be examined in terms of several factor, namely: (i) cost, 
(ii) time, (iii) risks and (iv) safety. Ultimately, the advantages of 
contingency planning enhance the chances of the organization's 
survival during a time of crisis. However, the limitations or 
disadvantage also need to be considered in order to determine 
the impact of contingency planning on an organization

subject: Business Management
content:
. 
{i} Cost 
The public can be quite forgiving, especially if crises are beyond 
the control of a business. By contrast, untruthful and deceitful 
cover-up stories are frowned upon by the public and the mass 
media. Acting in a socially responsible way (see Chapter 3) can 
be a source of competitive advantage. Contingency plans can 
therefore help to minimize negative reactions and hence the 
costs (financial losses) of crises should they ever occur. 
However, crises may never happen, so the time and money 
invested in contingency planning could have been better 
used elsewhere. Besides, no amount of planning can prevent 
the totally unexpected, such as natural disasters. Hence, over 
planning and over budgeting for crises can be inefficient use of 
a firm's scarce resources. 
570 
{ii} Time 
Planning takes time but can save time in the event of a crisis. 
Would you know exactly what to do if you were at school and 
an uncontrollable fire breaks out? What about in the event of 
a lockdown if an intruder were to attack the school? Prompt 
action is imperative to minimizing the impact of crises and the 
disaster recovery process. Delays in responding to a crisis can 
allow problems to escalate beyond repair

subject: Business Management
content:
. 
However, contingency planning uses up valuable management 
time and resources, thereby preventing senior managers to focus 
on other strategic priorities. It is also impossible to consider all 
scenarios; the more 'what if' situations that are considered, the 
more time that is spent on devising contingency plans. Time 
and resources are also needed to monitor, review and update 
these plans, including funds and time devoted to staff training 
to deal with potential crises. 
{iii) Risks 
Advocates of contingency planning argue that it helps to reduce 
risks as most potential threats or eventualities can be accounted 
for. A well-thought-out plan that can be easily followed in the 
event of a disaster helps to reduce overall risks. In the event of 
a catastrophic loss (such as injury or death), then the directors, 
managers or employees may be held personally or severally liable 
if company policies and guidelines were not followed, including 
possible non-compliance of health and safety legislation. 
However, if plans are based on outdated information or 
inaccurate data, then inappropriate actions may be taken if a 
crisis occurs. Contingency plans, no matter how detailed and 
well thought out, do not guarantee the survival of the business 
or the safety of its people

subject: Business Management
content:
. There is also the risk that people 
outside of the contingency planning team do not take things so 
seriously (perhaps due to ignorance), which severely limits the 
advantages of producing these plans. 
{iv) Safety 
Immediate actions, such as communications with the 
organization's personnel, can help to alleviate or minimize the 
concerns of staff and meet their security needs (see Chapter 
10). For example, most schools produce risk assessments for 
educational field trips, sporting activities and other outdoor 
pursuits. As part of a contingency plan, the risk assessments 
are produced to keep students and teachers as safe as possible, 
helping staff to know what to do in the event of an emergency. 
Contingency plans help in the process of effective handling

procedures can be overly complex and bureaucratic. For 
example, instructions for emergency evacuation of a building 
in the event of a fire may be disproportionately excessive, so 
such plans are inefficient and impractical in the event of a real 
crisis.

5.7 Crisis management and contingency planning (HL only) 
Crisis management, contingency 
planning and the key concepts 
A crisis is a threat to the sustainability of any business. Crisis 
management is about dealing with the changes that these 
threats bring. Contingency plans can go some way to deal with 
crises. With any crisis, it is the planned prevention ( contingency 
planning) and the proactive response of managers that 
minimize the impacts and changes caused by a crisis. To be of 
any use, the contingency plans must be properly and regularly 
tested, reviewed and updated based on any new information 
and changes in the internal and external environments. The 
crisis coordinator, usually a senior executive, works closely 
with a crisis management team and external agencies (such 
as lawyers, the press and the emergency services) to develop 
effective crisis management systems and processes. 
Crises change the environment in which a business operates, 
so effective crisis management can be vital for its survival. Yet, 
it is questionable whether and how much time and resources 
should be devoted to planning for events that may never 
happen. Moreover, some risks are simply not quantifiable, so 
dedicating management time and resources to contingency 
planning may not be regarded as cost effective or efficient use 
of scarce funds

subject: Business Management
content:
. Even if a detailed plan does exist, given the 
unpredictable nature of crises, it is possible that businesses do 
not act according to plans once they actually face a real crisis. 
Whatever the approach, it is important to act swiftly and 
transparently in an ethical way should a crisis occur. The 
mistakes of businesses such as Perrier and Bausch & Lomb 
have shown that immediate and transparent action can allow 
managers to take control of the situation in an ethical manner. 
How a business acts in a crisis can also raise ethical issues. For 
example, US regulators fined South Korea's Asiana Airlines 
$500,000 in 2014 for failing to help victims of a flight that 
crashed at San Francisco airport a year earlier. However, such 
responses require both careful contingency planning and an 
effective crisis management team to execute the plan. Only a 
properly trained representative should handle the media as the 
organization's official spokesperson. Any crisis could damage 
the corporate image of a business and reduce stakeholder 
confidence in the organization. Hence, contingency planning 
and crisis management often involve a strong focus on public 
relations (PR) aimed at establishing and protecting the desired 
corporate image

Research and development (R&D) refers to the technological 
and scientific research that helps to generate a flow of 
new commercial ideas and processes

subject: Business Management
content:
. It involves activities 
undertaken to innovate and introduce new goods and services 
or to improve existing ones to meet the needs of customers, 
of which they may or may not be aware. The purpose of R&D 
is to provide continual advancement (e.g., modifications or 
improvements to existing products) and to launch new products 
to satisfy customer needs in a profitable way. 
R&D often involves conducting extensive research into new 
products, their designs, testing and development of prototypes 
(trial or test products). Prototypes are designed, tested and 
developed with the hope of eventual commercial production. 
However, the R&D process can be extremely lengthy and drain 
the resources of a business. Furthermore, due to the high risks 
involved, only the most promising ones are considered for 
commercialization. For example, pharmaceutical companies 
often spend hundreds of millions of dollars each year on R&D, 
yet it can take more than a decade to commercialize a drug or 
medicine.

R&D can be vital to an organization's long-term survival 
and success. Kodak, for instance, went bankrupt after falling 
behind the times as customers switched from using camera film 
(see Figure 42.3) to digital camera technology. R&D can also 
improve the efficiency and performance of an organization, 
thereby adding value in the production process. For example, 
Apple and Microsoft have thrived on R&D as a source of higher 
sales growth and increased market value. Japanese carmaker 
Honda allocates 5% of its annual budget for R&D. 
R&D often pays off for businesses that operate in sunrise 
industries (those that have rapid growth potential, such as 
high-tech industries). In addition, R&D can generate a first-
mover advantage, i.e., the benefits of being the first business to 
launch a new and innovative product, such as Tesla's electric 
car (2012), Apple's iPod (October 2001) or Pfizer's Viagra 
impotence drug (March 1998). Such benefits include the ability 
to charge a premium price, to develop a favourable corporate 
image and to establish strong market share

subject: Business Management
content:
. Hence, having a 
first-mover advantage better prepares a business to contend 
with the likely competition that follows. By contrast, R&D 
expenditure in sunset industries (where there is negative or 
deteriorating growth potential) is unlikely to be profitable. 
Furthermore, studies have consistently shown that for every 
ten products that are developed and test-marketed, only one 
product reaches commercialization. Hence, the successful 
product that is launched must recoup the high costs of R&D, 
even if this takes several years. 
R&D is a continual process. American inventor Thomas Edison 
(1847 - 1931) said, "I have not failed. I've just found 10,000 ways 
that won't work:' Firms that continue to invest in R&D, even if 
everyone else is cutting back, perhaps due to a recession, are 
the ones most likely to thrive in the future. Successful R&D can 
give businesses a competitive edge in terms of cost advantages 
and/or quality improvements in the long term.

Question 42.1 - Nintendo Company 
Entering new markets - Ferrari has long faced the dilemma 
of wanting to sell more cars without damaging its image of 
exclusivity. Founded in 1947, Ferrari did not expand into 
China until 45 years later, allowing the Italian supercar 
maker to exceed its quota of 5,000 cars produced each year 
since the Chinese market does not affect the elitism enjoyed 
by Ferrari customers in Europe and North America. 
Management guru Peter Drucker said that all successful 
businesses at some point required a manager to make 
courageous decisions. He argued that businesses cannot grow 
through cost cutting alone but require R&D and innovation 
to sustain or increase their profitability. For instance, Apple's 
revolutionary iPod was introduced in October 2001 and in just 
5 years had sold over 60 million units worldwide. By early 2007, 
Apple had sold its 100 millionth iPod, significantly boosting the 
company's earnings. Nevertheless, the iPod was discontinued 
in 2014 due to the shift in customer preference for online 
streaming music services. As Ken Loh, Regional Director of 
Kalmar (a multinational B2B manufacturer of heavy industry

dependent on whether it will invest to meet customers' needs and 
expectations in order to increase competitiveness

Intellectual property protection 
Intellectual property protection: (i) copyrights, (ii) patents and (iii) 
trademarks. AO2 
© IBO, 2022 
I 
ntellectual property rights (IP Rs), also referred to 
as intellectual property protection, are the legal and 
exclusive ownership claims to certain creations, inventions 
or pieces of work

subject: Business Management
content:
. They act to prevent other parties from 
replicating the ideas of the inventor or creator. Hence, IPRs act 
as an incentive for businesses to innovate. Also, IPRs allow the 
owner to benefit from having a first-mover advantage as there 
is scope to take advantage of having a monopoly position in the 
market. The main types of IPR are (i) copyrights, (ii) patents 
and (iii) trademarks. 
(i} Copyrights 
Copyrights provide legal protection for artists and authors by 
preventing others from using or replicating their published 
works without permission. Governments grant the permission 
to hold copyrights for a finite period of time. Works that 
have been protected by copyright often carry the © symbol. 
Copyrights are popular in the music, film, drama, art, 
photography, software and publishing industries. 
Authors such as J.K. Rowling, Dan Brown and Stephen King 
have made their fortunes from selling their copyrighted works 
to large Hollywood movie studios. Rowling's highly successful 
Harry Potter books have earned her international fame and 
ensured she became the first person to earn over $1 billion from 
writing. 
Note: This textbook, whilst not in the same league as the authors 
above, is protected by international copyrights

subject: Business Management
content:
. Reproduction 
and redistribution in physical or electric format are strictly 
prohibited, irrespective of whether or not this is for financial 
gain. 
(ii) Patents 
A patent is the legal right to be the exclusive producer or user 
of a newly invented process or product, for a finite period of 
time. Patents existed as far back as 1449, when a patent was 
granted in the UK for the process of making stained glass 
windows. A patent is granted after the inventor has registered 
and satisfied the conditions stipulated by the government. Not 
all applications for a patent are approved, especially if the ideas 
are not new or are simply minor improvements to existing 
technologies or processes. 
Patents can be held by individuals or businesses as intangible 
assets (see Chapter 17). They do not come free of charge, so 
patents applications are only submitted for inventions that are 
likely to be commercially profitable over a long period of time. 
Ownership of the patent can then act as a barrier to entry as the 
patent prevents competitors from using the invention (without 
the prior consent of the patent holder). The patent holder is also 
entitled to sell the technology or invention to another business

subject: Business Management
content:
. 
A famous example of a patent holder is Dyson Limited. James 
Dyson pioneered the bag-free vacuum cleaner in 1978 and 
patented the technology five years later through licensing his 
invention in Japan. The invention made Dyson one of Britain's 
best known and wealthiest people. Dyson now sells highly 
innovative products throughout the world and has annual sales 
of over $8.2 billion.

(iii) Trademarks 
A trademark is a sign, slogan or logo that represents a business 
or a product belonging to that business. If the trademark is 
registered at a patent office, it acts as a barrier to rivals wanting 
to imitate the product name or symbol. Trademarks that have 
been registered can, but do not necessarily, carry the • symbol 
next to the mark. However, it is illegal to use this symbol if a 
trademark has not been registered. 
Trademarks are often used as a form of branding (see 
Chapter 27). For example, suggestive trademarks are used to 
give customers a hint about the nature or characteristic of a 
product, e.g., BMW's Mini (small).

subject: Business Management
content:
A descriptive trademark is 
used to show a direct link between the brand and the product, 
e.g., Pictionary and Monopoly board games. Finally, arbitrary 
trademarks are purely random and meaningless names, e.g., 
Apple computers or Haagen-Dazs ice cream.

Box 42.2 - Famous inventors and

Although there are technical differences between 
innovation and inventions, the terms are often used 
interchangeably. Examples of famous inventors and their

Innovation can be categorised as incremental or disruptive. 
(i) Incremental innovation 
Incremental innovation refers to minor improvements 
to products, services or work processes. For example, car 
manufacturers might work on developing safer and more 
energy efficient vehicles. Gillette, the world's largest producer 
of shaving supplies, regularly upgrades its razors, adding 
new features such as extra blades and pivoting functions. 
The majority of innovations are incremental in nature as 
they are more affordable, of lower risk and less disruptive to 
organizations.

5.8 Research and Development (HL only) 
Theory of Knowledge (TOK) 
To what extent is research and development (R&D) 
limited by ethical considerations? 
Research & Development and the 
key concepts 
The pace of change in certain industries means that effective 
R&D expenditure is increasingly important. When cameras 
were first invented, there was very limited competition, so 
manufacturers enjoyed stability in the industry. Over time, 
with the invention of 35mm camera film, the market became 
dominated by market leaders such as Kodak, Minolta and Fuji. 
Competition led to continuous improvements that fuelled R&D. 
However, with the introduction of digital cameras and then 
mobile devices with digital camera functions, competition has 
intensified to a global level with R&D focusing on continuous 
innovations. 
Stability becomes less certain in an ever-changing business 
world. R&D can certainly be the catalyst for change. For example, 
the first edition of the Encyclopaedia Britannica was printed in 
Edinburgh, Scotland but it finally went out of print in 2012 after 
244 years. This was the harsh reality of the digital age, including 
competition from open sources like Wikipedia.

subject: Business Management
content:
Although 
Faber-Castell has over 260 years of history in producing pens 
and pencils, is it simply a matter of time before we no longer 
need to use pens and pencils? The 1B will eventually replace 
paper-based exams with online assessments. Hence, the ability 
to adapt to and manage changes in the business environment 
will enable organizations to achieve better customer satisfaction 
and hence to sustain or improve their profitability. 
Figure 42.6 - How long will it be before these products 
become innovations of yesteryear? 
In rapidly changing markets, such as the movie industry or the 
computer games market, R&D and innovation are key factors 
to business longevity and financial success. Product life cycles 
(see Chapter 27) in these markets are very short and consumer 
demand is continually changing ( demanding 'better' and more 
exciting films and computer games, for example). In addition, 
production costs tend to be very high, thereby making the risk 
of failure a real threat. Therefore, innovation is paramount in 
these industries. Seeking new market opportunities is a crucial 
source of innovation, e.g., downloading television programmes, 
movies and computer games onto smartphones and portable 
media players

subject: Business Management
content:
. 
Essentially, businesses that are able to embrace change are more 
likely to survive and thrive, especially in industries where the 
life cycle of many products is short. Hence, any effective and 
creative business strategy is likely to include R&D expenditure 
to ensure the organization copes with changes and disruptions 
in the external environment. 
Business Management Toolkit 
To what extent does corporate culture impact R&D? 
You may want to refer to Chapters 11 and 54 before 
addressing this question. 
Ethical considerations may also influence R&D practices and 
strategies. Most governments encourage R&D and innovation 
through the protection of intellectual property rights (IPRs). 
Not only is it unethical to infringe the IPRs of others, but it is 
also illegal. However, IPRs have become of greater concern to 
many businesses due to developments in Internet and online 
technologies. Some countries do not have laws governing the 
use of IPR on the Internet, for example. The common practice 
of music and video downloads, for instance, is still very 
challenging for governments to enforce. The United Nation's 
World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) has gone 
some way to encourage and promote the protection of IPRs 
around the world

subject: Business Management
content:
. However, the existence of non-complying 
and non-participating countries presents somewhat of a 
challenge for multinational companies and the WIPO. This can 
threaten the sustainability of some businesses so often deters 
R&D expenditure. 
There are also huge ethical issues and implications of how 
R&D is conducted. For example, cosmetic companies might 
test their products on animals or dispose of their wastes in 
unenvironmentally friendly ways. Similarly, R&D can impact 
on the ethical practices of organizations. For example, many

Ultimately, R&D can help to address the unmet needs of 
customers. It is at the heart of problem-solving and is a major

Topic 5: Operations management 
Types of data analytics include: 
Descriptive data analytics, which describes and answers 
questions about what has happened over a period of time. 
It can help to keep track of business successes and failures 
as well as providing essential insights into past business 
performance. For example, data can be used to describe 
what has happened to a firm's sales revenues over a given 
period of time. 
Diagnostic data analytics, which focuses on and answers 
questions about why something has happened. It goes 
beyond finding out what has happened by determining the 
cause and examining why it has happened. For example, to 
determine the extent to which a promotional campaign or 
change in pricing method has impacted sales volume. 
Predictive data analytics, which projects and answers 
questions about what is likely to happen in the foreseeable 
future. For example, this approach enables managers to 
extrapolate data and make more realistic sales forecasts by 
using historical data to identify trends. Such techniques 
include the use of simple linear regression (see Chapter 58). 
Prescriptive data analytics, which supports strategic 
planning and an appropriate course of action by answering 
questions about what should be done

subject: Business Management
content:
. For example, if data 
analytics suggests a high likelihood of warmer summer 
evenings, restaurants may need to order more food and 
drinks, as well as hire more staff in anticipation of more 
diners. 
Essentially, data analytics is important because it helps 
businesses to improve their efficiency, cut costs and gain 
competitive advantages in order to increase their profits. It 
enables businesses to gain insights that were not previously 
accessible in order to establish new patterns and correlations 
in large data sets. Data-driven decisions are more objective (as 
they are based on evidence) so help to reduce risks. Having large 
amounts of data and relevant information enables businesses 
to improve their performance, such as helping to identify 
consumer trends and raising customer satisfaction by providing 
new and better-quality goods and services. Ultimately, data 
analytics can be used to make more informed business decisions 
notwithstanding uncertainties in the economy.

Database (A01) 
A database is a computerized system that makes it easy to store, 
search and select data and information. In the same way that a 
public library stores a large range of books, a database stores a 
large volume of data and information that is used by a business

subject: Business Management
content:
. 
With computerised systems and structures, businesses can 
input, organize, save, protect and retrieve data in an efficient 
way (in terms of speed and accuracy). 
Businesses will typically use databases to keep track of 
information about customers, employees, inventory (stock) 
and accounting information. For example, a shoe retailer that 
sells a range of different types of footwear will need to keep 
records of the sales of the different shoes sold (such as the type, 
size and colour of the shoes) as well as important details about 
the customers. Similarly, schools are likely to use a database to 
keep track of each student's personal details, such as their name, 
age, year group, home address, details of the parents or legal 
guardians, medical records, attendance and punctuality records 
and emergency contact details. Schools will also have a similar 
database for their staff, as well as records of their ongoing 
professional training and career development. 
In the digital age, the disadvantages of using databases are 
minimal, but include the initial set-up costs as well as ongoing 
maintenance costs, such as the cost of hiring database managers. 
There is also the potential risk of cybersecurity (see below)

subject: Business Management
content:
. 
Nevertheless, the reliance of businesses on accurate financial 
records, secure credit card accounts, efficient billing and 
invoicing and important customer records are all valid reasons 
why databases are so important for businesses.

Cybersecurity and cybercrime 
(A01) 
Cybersecurity refers to the protection of computer systems and 
networks from unwarranted information disclosure, as well as 
theft of or damage to computer hardware, software or data. It is 
used to protect businesses and individuals against cybercrime. 
Cybercrime refers to any illegal activity carried out using 
computers or the Internet by deliberately and maliciously 
targeting computers, computer networks or networked devices. 
Cybercrime can be carried out by individuals or organizations 
and is usually done for financial reasons (profit), but in some 
cases can be caused by political or personal motives. 
With the increased reliance on e-commerce and the growing 
popularity of a cashless society, cybercrime is becoming more 
Figure 43.2 - Cybersecurity is an increasingly important issue 
of a threat to people and businesses across the world. Examples 
for businesses 
of interrelated cybercrime include: 
Phishing - This is the use of fraudulent messages designed 
by the attacker to trick victims into revealing sensitive 
information. 
Ransomware - This is the use of malicious software from 
cybercriminals who threaten to publish the victim's 
personal data or permanently block access to the data 
unless a ransom is paid to the attackers

subject: Business Management
content:
. 
Email and internet fraud - This refers to the use of enticing 
messages in emails and text messages, such as "Tap on this 
link and claim your $1 million today!" 
Identity theft - This occurs when an individual's private 
information is stolen and used without any permission. 
Account hijacking - This occurs when an individual's 
private or profession account (such as email, social media 
or bank account) is stolen and abused or misused. This 
includes hijacking a company's website and shutting it 
down completely. 
• 
Intellectual property theft - This is the piracy or theft of 
materials that legally belong to others, such as copyright 
infringements and counterfeiting of registered trademarks 
(see Chapter 42). 
Businesses can protect themselves against cybercrimes by 
improving their cybersecurity systems and processes. This 
includes methods such as: 
Keeping computer software, network structures and 
operating system updated. 
Using anti-virus software to prevent or limit the volume of 
cyberattacks. 
Training staff about the importance of cybersecurity and 
practical strategies such as: 
o 
never opening unsolicited email attachments 
o 
using stronger security passwords (and updating these 
at appropriate times) and 
o 
being extremely cautious when disclosing private or 
confidential information

{i} Artificial neural networks 
Artificial neural networks (ANN) are a form of machine-
learning that use learning algorithms that can independently 
make adjustments as they receive new input. This means that 
ANNs can solve problems without having to be explicitly 
programmed with rules to follow, in a similar way to that of the 
human brain. This means ANNs are the basic building blocks of 
artificial intelligence (AI). 
ANNs can be used for many business applications, such as 
natural language processing in chatbots (used for interacting 
online with customers) and predictive analysis for detecting 
spam email and phishing text messages. 
Inspired by the structure of the human brain, artificial neural 
networks are used to make computers or machines more 
human like in terms of their use of reasoning, intuition and 
even imagination

subject: Business Management

. ANNs were first developed back in the 1950s 
to address the issue that computers cannot interpret the context 
of real-world situations or apply common sense to problems in 
the way that human brains are capable of. 
Examples of business applications of artificial neural networks 
include: 
Google uses ANN learning algorithms to make its 'watch 
next' recommendations for YouTube videos. 
Facebook uses ANNs for its DeepFace facial recognition 
system, which uses algorithms to recognize faces with 
around 97% accuracy. 
Microsoft's Skype uses ANN to do translations of live 
online conversations.

{iii) Cloud computing 
Cloud computing is similar to data centres except that it is a 
virtual resource or online space that enables businesses to store, 
organize and retrieve data in safe and efficient ways. As with 
data centres, cloud computing requires the use of computer 
networks and remote servers, which possess a unique function. 
However, there has been a shift in critical infrastructure from 
traditional on-premises physical servers in data centres to virtual 
networks that support work applications and data management 
in a cloud environment. The 'cloud' is not a physical entity but 
a virtual service and is accessed via an Internet connection. At 
the most basic level, cloud computing storage services include 
Google Drive, Microsoft One Drive, iCloud and Dropbox. 
Other examples of cloud services providers for businesses

The Internet of Things (loT) refers to a broad system of transfer or sharing of data. 
physical objects embedded with electronics, software and 
sensors that connect to the Internet. These devices are able 
to collect, transfer and store huge volumes of data over the 
Internet in real time. Hence, the physical objects ( or 'things') 
are also referred to connected devices through wireless and 
Bluetooth technologies. Examples include smart devices (such 
as smartphones, smart heating systems, office security devices 
and home appliances) as well as wearable technologies.

For example, in the healthcare industry, wearable smart devices 
are an application of the IoT. They can be used to keep records 
of health-related data for health clinics, hospitals and health 
insurance providers. Doctors or surgeons, for example, can use 
a large volume of statistical data of their patients so that the best 
form of treatment can be applied in a timely manner

subject: Business Management

Car manufacturers and car dealerships use data from each vehicle 
to offer customers an appointment for servicing (maintenance), 
to get their parts fixed, send customers directions to the nearest 
dealer or garage and make sure the correct replacement parts 
are ordered so they are ready for when the customer arrives. 
Hence, the loT helps businesses to operate in a more lean and 
efficient way (see Chapter 37) and can generate significant 
competitive advantages. 
The purpose behind the Internet of Things is for connected 
devices that self-report in real-time so that the data can be 
used to improve efficiency. It removes the need to depend on 
human intervention to collect, process and interpret important 
information. Moreover, the loT is able to do this far more 
quickly and accurately, in real-time. 
The Internet of Things generates massive volumes of data 
from countless devices that are permanently connected to the 
Internet. The personal and business possibilities of this are only 
limited by imagination and creativity. However, due to the vast 
Case study 43.1 - Smart devices 
Amazon's Alexa, Google's Home and Apple's Siri (digital 
voice assistants) are examples of widely used consumer

lives of billions of people

. Users can talk to digital voice 
assistants like Alexa for a wide and growing variety of 
functions including playing music on demand, reporting 
live news coverage, providing weather reports, asking 
questions about literally any topic, calling family and 
friends, setting reminders and alarms, ordering an Uber 
and so much more. 
The main advantage of the loT is that it improves efficiency 
(minimizing human effort and saving time to get tasks done). 
Enhanced data collection and access to real-time information

concerns. There could also be concerns about the growing 
dependency on the Internet and hence the inability for

ability to boost operational efficiency and complete highly 
complex tasks that cannot be easily managed by human beings

Case study 43.4 - Data mining and 
customer loyalty programmes 
Retailers such as supermarkets are established users of 
data mining techniques. Many supermarkets offer free 
loyalty programmes to customers. Loyalty cards are used 
to offer customers reduced prices and special offers that 
are not available to non-members. The magnetic strips 
on customer loyalty cards make it easy for retailers to 
track what customers are buying, the quantities in which 
they buy these, when they are buying the products and 
at what price. After mining the data, supermarket stores 
can then use this information to execute more suitable 
marketing strategies to target and retain their customers. 
However, the use of data mining has come under scrutiny 
and criticism especially when users, employees or customers 
are unaware of their data being collected and mined, often 
for commercial gain. The selling, sharing or redistribution of 
personal information without the prior knowledge and approval 
of owners is unethical and illegal in many countries, especially 
when the data are used to influence preferences and decision 
making

anagement Information Systems (MIS) refers 
to the study of advanced computer technologies

Employees want to maintain their privacy while employers

The Ansoff matrix is a framework of generic growth strategies for a business, based on 
providing new or existing products in new or existing markets. These four generic growth 
strategies are categorised as (i) market penetration, (ii) market development, (iii) product 
development and (iv) diversification. 
This framework considers factors in the external environment that affect a business. 
STEEPLE refers to the social, technological, economic, environmental, political, legal and

SWOT analysis 
The Business Management toolkit is a set of 
situational, planning and decision-making tools 
used to analyse and evaluate the syllabus content

analysis is a situation tool. Chapter references have been included

© IBO, 2022 
Figure 44.1 - SWOT analysis is a commonly used situational 
tool 
SWOT analysis is a situational tool used to assess the internal 
strengths and weaknesses and the external opportunities and 
threats of a business. SWOT is an acronym for Strengths, 
Weaknesses, Opportunities and Threats. It can be used to 
assess the current situation of a business or organization. 
SWOT analysis considers both internal factors (strengths and 
weaknesses) and external factors (opportunities and threats) 
that are relevant to the organization under consideration. 
Strengths are internal factors that are favourable compared 
with competitors, such as strong brand loyalty, a good 
corporate image or highly skilled workers

subject: Business Management
content:
. Strengths help 
the business to better achieve its organizational objectives 
(see Chapter 3). Hence, strengths need to be developed and 
protected. 
Weaknesses are internal factors that are unfavourable 
when compared to rivals. Such factors create competitive 
disadvantages. Weaknesses are therefore likely to prevent 
or delay the business from achieving its goals. Hence, 
to remain competitive, the business needs to reduce or 
remove its weaknesses. 
Opportunities are the external possibilities (prospects) 
for future development. Such factors refer to changes in 
the external environment that create favourable conditions 
for a business. For example, India and China present 
many business opportunities for multinational companies 
(see Chapter 6), such as a huge customer base and rapid 
economic growth. Hence, SWOT analysis can help 
organizations to formulate their business strategies. 
Threats are the external factors that hinder the prospects 
for an organization. Hence, threats cause problems for the 
business. Examples include technological breakdowns, 
product defects and recalls (see Chapter 40), changes in 
fashion, price wars (Chapter 28), oil crises, recessions, 
natural disasters and the outbreak of infectious diseases

Exam tip! 
When carrying out a SWOT analysis, remember that: 
Strengths and weaknesses are the internal factors 
that an organization currently faces. 
Opportunities and threats are the external factors that 
the organization is likely to face in the foreseeable 
future. 
Developing business strategies 
based on SWOT analyses 
SWOT analysis can be an extremely useful situational tool for 
investigating all sorts of business situations as part of strategic 
planning and decision making. For example, it can be used to 
provide a framework for: 
Competitor analysis, such as the threats posed by a 
competitor or the strengths of a rival. 
Assessing opportunities, such as the development and 
growth prospects for the organization. 
Risk assessment, such as the probable effects of investing in 
a certain project or location. 
Reviewing corporate strategy, such as the market position or 
strategic direction of the business. 
Strategic planning, such as the decision to diversify or 
expand in oversea markets. 
Once a SWOT analysis is completed, appropriate business 
strategies can be identified and discussed to deal with potential 
situations in a more optimal way based on the organization's 
identified strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and threats

subject: Business Management
content:
. In 
particular, organizations should strive to: 
Build on their organizational strengths. 
Reverse their weaknesses. 
Maximize their responses to business opportunities. 
Overcome threats to their businesses. 
BMT 1 - SWOT Analysis 
Just investigating the strengths, weaknesses, opportunities and 
threats alone is of minimal value to managers and decision 
makers. From a SWOT analysis, four basic strategies can be 
identified. 
Opportunities 
Threats 
Strengths 
Offensive 
Defensive 
Weaknesses

Survival 
Figure 44.2 - SWOT analysis and business strategies 
Offensive strategies - The ideal situation occurs if a strength 
meets an opportunity as this enables the business to gain 
maximum benefit from a favourable external situation, 
i.e., the business should make the most of the favourable 
situation. 
Defensive strategies - In this case, a strength meets an 
external threat, so the situation presents an element of risk, 
which requires the business to defend itself. Typically, this 
strategy involves the business paying close attention to 
the competition so that it does not lose market share (see 
Chapter 23) or hinder its market dominance. 
Reorientation strategies - In this case, there is a favourable 
situation in the external environment, but which correlates 
to an internal weakness

subject: Business Management
content:
. Hence, the business needs to 
adjust or reorient its policies and practices. For example, 
this strategy could involve the business trying to cut costs 
to improve its liquidity position (see Chapter 18), remain 
competitive and gain market share. 
Survival strategies - The most undesirable situation occurs 
if a weakness meets an external threat. Survival policies are 
aimed at minimising the adverse effects of such a situation. 
This means that the business has to pay maximum attention 
to avoid a disastrous outcome and to survive. 
Finally, it is important to remember that SWOT analysis does 
not guarantee that a strategy will be successful. For example, 
identifying weaknesses and threats does not necessarily mean 
that the business has sufficient financial and human resources 
to tackle these risks.

Exam tip! 
When using a SWOT analysis in the exam, do not present 
the SWOT in tabular form. Using such a format can 
encourage you to squeeze your answers to fit inside 
a table that you have drawn. Examiners prefer written 
explanations and justifications. It is acceptable to write 
in bullet point format under each SWOT heading so long 
as the examiner can understand the reasoning behind 
your arguments. 
Exam tip! 
A common exam question will require you to examine the 
current position of a business by using a SWOT analysis 
framework. Therefore, be sure to learn how to use a SWOT 
analysis properly. Remember that the strengths and 
weaknesses refer to the current and internal position of 
the organization. The opportunities and threats should 
stem from a STEEPLE analysis of the external environment 
(see Chapter 46, Business Management Toolkit 3). 
Evaluation of SWOT analysis 
SWOT analyses often lack quantitative assessment, with no 
value for the costs of addressing an identified weakness or 
potential rewards from pursuing an identified opportunity. 
Unlike some other tools, such as decision trees and force field 
analysis (see Chapters 49 and 55 respectively), the use of SWOT 
analysis does not prioritise issues for managers and decision 
makers

subject: Business Management

. 
Typically, SWOT analysis cannot be used in isolation. After all, 
a SWOT analysis only assesses the current situation and does 
not suggest any actual strategy. Better decisions are made if 
more information is available, so other tools may be required 
to achieve this. Nevertheless, as it encourages managers to 
think holistically and collaboratively, SWOT analysis can help 
to reduce the overall risks of decision-making by demanding 
objective, more informed and logical thought processes.

Figure 45.1 - The Ansoff Matrix 
(i) Market penetration 
Market penetration is the growth strategy that involves a 
business choosing to focus on selling existing products in 
existing markets, i.e., to increase their market share of current 
products. Hence, this is a relatively low-risk growth strategy. 
Market penetration might be achieved by offering more 
competitive prices (see Chapter 28) or by improved advertising 
(see Chapter 29) to enhance the desirability of the product. In 
addition to attracting more customers, firms might attempt to 
entice existing customers to buy more frequently, perhaps by 
offering customer loyalty schemes (see Chapter 43). Brands 
might also be repositioned (see Chapter 24) to achieve market 
penetration. 
An advantage of market penetration is that the business focuses 
on markets and products that it is familiar with. Hence, market 
research expenditure (see Chapter 26) can be minimised. It is 
also the safest of the four growth strategies. 
A limitation of market penetration is that competitors, 
especially stronger rivals, are likely to retaliate to any business 
trying to take away their customers and market share

lead to aggressive reactions, such as price wars (see Chapter 
28), thereby harming profits in the short term at least. Also, 
once existing markets become saturated, alternative growth 
strategies are required if the business is to continue its growth 
and evolution.

{ii} Product development 
Product development is a growth strategy that involves selling 
new products in existing markets. Hence, this strategy carries 
a medium level of risk for the business. Apple's launch of the 
iPhone in 2007 revolutionised the mobile phone industry and 
propelled the profits for the computer manufacturer founded 
in 1976. McDonald's often adds new products to its menu. 
Car manufacturers introduce new models and occasionally 
limited editions of their cars. These are all examples of product 
development growth strategies. 
Figure 45.2 - McDonald's product development strategy 
involves new additions to its menu 
Product development tends to rely heavily on product 
extension strategies to prolong the demand for goods and 
services that have reached the saturation or decline stage of 
their product life cycle (see Chapter 27). Product development 
is also reliant on brand development to appeal to the existing 
market. For example, well-established companies such as Sony 
or Nike can use their brand names to launch new products to 
the market as there are fewer risks of introducing a new product 
under a well-known and trusted brand

{iii} Market development 
Market development is the growth strategy that involves selling 
existing products in new markets, i.e., an established product is 
marketed to a new set of customers. This might be done through 
new distribution channels such as selling the existing product 
overseas (although this could be quite risky if the business 
is unfamiliar with local market conditions and cultures). 
Alternatively, promotional strategies could be tweaked to 
make the product more appealing to the new audience. Pricing 
methods (see Chapter 28) could also be changed to attract 
different market segments. 
A key advantage of this growth strategy is that the business 
is familiar with the product that is being marketed. For 
example, Nike and Adidas successfully market their clothing 
products for leisure rather than specifically for sports. Nokia 
uses market development to sell its excess supply of mass-
produced smartphones that have a short product life cycle in 
more economically developed countries (where customers 
frequently upgrade their devices) by selling these in lower 
income countries such as Sri Lanka, Indonesia and Nigeria

necessarily guarantee its success in other markets. Market

presence. American retail giant Target closed more than 130

differences (see Chapter 11). Google struggled to establish itself 
in China, where local company Baidu maintains around 85% 
market share.

new products in new markets. For example, the Virgin Group

to spread risks by having a well-balanced product portfolio (see

growth. 
One way to diversify is to become a holding company. This is

"The reasonable man adapts himself to the world; the unreasonable one persists in trying to adapt the world to himself." 
- George Bernard Shaw (1856 - 1950), Irish author 
STEEPLE analysis 
The Business Management toolkit is a set of 
situational, planning and decision-making tools 
used to analyse and evaluate the syllabus content as 
well as being applied in different contexts. STEEPLE 
analysis is a situation tool.

TEEPLE is an acronym for the Social, Technological, 
Economic, Environmental, Political, Legal and Ethical 
opportunities and threats in the external business 
environment. These factors, unlike internal ones, affect 
all businesses yet are beyond the control of any individual 
organization. STEEPLE analysis is a situation tool that is central 
to formulating business strategy, such as assessing the feasibility 
of an overseas investment project. 
External factors that represent prospects for businesses are 
called opportunities, such as lower tax rates and lower interest 
rates. External factors that can harm a business are called 
threats, such as a recession, oil crisis or major road works

Worked example - STEEPLE analysis of multinational companies operating in India 
Social factors 
Potential market of over 1.38 billion people (the second most populous country in the world) 
• A large and well-educated English-speaking workforce of around 130 million people. 
Large yet increasing discrepancies in the distribution of income and wealth. 
Language barriers in rural cities, with potential clash of national cultures in a multilingual and multi-ethnic country. 
Technological factors 
Growing number of technologically aware population (huge opportunities for firms providing products such as mobile 
phones, personal computers, and Internet services). Bengaluru, the IT capital of India, is widely regarded as the "Silicon 
Valley of India''. 
Major industries include communications technology, biotechnology, computer software, automobiles, petrochemicals, 
and pharmaceuticals. 
Technologies are easily copied due to a lack of appropriate legislation. 
Economic factors 
Huge growth potential in financial markets. 
Significant economic growth and rising disposable incomes (spending power) in India

subject: Business Management

. 
Improved infrastructure and market opportunities in cities such as Mumbai, Bengaluru, and New Delhi. 
Relatively low costs of production (average wage rates are still very low). 
Most people are employed in the agricultural sector, with India being one of the world's top producers of cereals (wheat, 
rice and sugar), meat, fruits, vegetables, tea, coffee, cotton, coal and wool. 
Infrastructure and economic stability are less attractive than in other countries such as China and the United Arab 
Emirates. 
The vast majority of the Indian population is still very poor, with a real GDP per capital of less than $2,000 in 2022. 
Environmental factors 
Major challenges for India include tackling air pollution, water pollution, littering, waste disposal and environmental 
degradation. 
The Indian government is taking a more proactive approach to enforcing environmental protection. 
Political factors 
• Political reform in India will encourage better trade relations with other nations. 
Legislation is less stringent than in other nations, thus placing fewer constraints on business activity. 
Regarded as less politically stable and relatively corrupt compared with other countries in the region

subject: Business Management

Legal factors 
• Strict compliance laws for foreign bank accounts and heavy penalties for tax evasion. 
Employment legislation is often overlooked, such as poaching of staff from competitors is commonplace. 
There are no specific data protection laws enforced in India . 
Ethical factors 
Corruption is widespread, which does little to help combat poverty and can harm India's international competitiveness. 
Slow business negotiations because establishing a trusting relationship is a prerequisite to doing business in India. 
Indian culture is averse to critical disagreements, such as saying 'no; as this is seen as being rather rude; disagreements 
should be expressed in an ethical way, using diplomatic language. 
It can be difficult for foreign businesses to penetrate the Indian economy without partnering with a local Indian company.

subject: Business Management
content:
The importance of each opportunity and threat identified in a 
STEEPLE analysis can be weighted in a scientific or objective 
way. This is useful when trying to examine the advantages and 
disadvantages of a decision. If the overall importance placed 
on the opportunities of a decision outweigh the threats, then 
the business is likely to pursue that option. However, in reality, 
external factors are subject to rapid and unforeseeable change. 
An external shock, such as a global pandemic or a financial 
crisis, can jeopardize the chances of success despite what a 
STEEPLE analysis initially revealed. 
A key advantage of STEEPLE analysis is that it is relatively 
simple to use. The analysis helps managers to be thorough 
and logical in their analysis of the external opportunities and 
threats faced by the business. It is also a useful situational tool 
for brainstorming and discussions. STEEPLE analysis promotes 
proactive and forward thinking, rather than static views based 
on gut feelings. Hence, it is more likely that managers will 
be better informed and prepared to deal with changes in the 
external environment. 
Exam tip! 
It is not always necessary to conduct a full STEEPLE 
analysis

to use a PEST analysis, where political factors include 
(where appropriate) legal opportunities and threats, 
and social factors include ethical and environmental

Technological opportunities and 
threats (STEEPLE analysis) 
The technological environment refers to scientific knowledge 
and application to the external environment that presents 
constant threats and opportunities. Advances in technology 
and work processes have improved productivity. For example, 
Internet technologies (see Table 46.1) create countless 
opportunities for entrepreneurs to set up and run their 
businesses without some of the financial risks of establishing 
a physical business. Success stories include Mark Zuckerberg 
(Facebook), Kevin Systrom (Instagram), Reed Hastings and 
Marc Randolph (Netflix), Zhang Yiming (Tik Tok) and Eric 
Yuan (Zoom). 
However, the high cost of staying up to date with technological 
progress can cause problems for businesses. For example, 
Airbus faced lengthy delays in the production of the A380 
(the world's largest commercial aircraft) and subsequently had 
to compensate its customers such as Emirates Airlines and 
Singapore Airlines. 
Technology affects all aspects of business functions. For 
instance, the Internet has directly affected Human Resource 
Management (in the recruitment process), Marketing (such as 
e-commerce), Finance (annual reports are published online) 
and Operations Management (such as access to benchmarking 
data)

subject: Business Management
content:
. 
BMT 3 - STEEPLE analysis 
Apart from the Internet, other opportunities that technology 
can bring to businesses include: 
New working practices - Many more businesses are 
using flexible working practices (see Chapter 7), such as 
enabling people to work from home, by using Information 
Communication Technology (ICT). Global businesses are 
also increasingly using video conferencing to cut the costs 
of face-to-face meetings and international recruitment. 
Marketing activities have also been affected, such as the 
growing popularity of online advertising. 
Increased productivity and efficiency gains - Robots and 
machines are much faster yet more accurate than humans, 
especially in the mass production of products over 
prolonged periods of time. Unlike humans, machinery 
can be made to work for very long hours without the need 
for breaks, financial rewards, motivation or maternity 
leave! Firms are also more likely to achieve zero defects 
(no wastage) from the use of technology (see Chapter 40). 
Automated stock control systems can automatically re-
order stocks. Despite the large initial costs of automation 
and technology, capital-intensive firms can benefit from 
cost savings in the long run

subject: Business Management

. 
Quicker product development times - The use of CAD/CAM 
technology (computer aided design and computer aided 
manufacturing) has allowed firms to produce prototypes 
in a timely and cost-effective way, thereby accelerating the 
design, manufacturing and launch of new products. 
Table 46.1 - Opportunities and threats of internet technologies 
Opportunities 
Speed of access to information - Businesses and customers can 
gain access to up-to-date information from any part of the 
world through dedicated websites, such as the huge range of 
online news media sources that give invaluable information to 
users in a cost-effective way. 
Reducing language and cultural barriers - Information on the 
Internet can be easily translated into different languages by 
using dedicated software or translators. This can also help to 
reduce the costs of trading overseas. 
Reduced costs - Firms with an online presence can benefit 
immensely from e-commerce. Trading can take place at any 
time from any part of the world without the need for a physical 
outlet. Therefore, labour costs can also be reduced. 
Overcoming geographical limitations - The Internet makes 
location less of an issue for many businesses

subject: Business Management

. The increasing 
use of mobile devices has fuelled e-commerce and literally 
eliminated any limitations of geographical proximity to physical 
retailers. 
Threats 
Price transparency -
Firms are exposed to the forces of 
competition as customers can easily compare the prices of 
different businesses without leaving their home or office. In 
addition, as there is no physical presence, it can be difficult to 
judge a product's quality relative to the price. 
Online crime - Hackers have cost e-commerce businesses a 
huge amount of money. Online banking scams and credit card 
fraud are quite common. This threat has therefore restricted the 
number of online customers. 
Higher production costs - In addition to the costs of online crime, 
businesses also face maintenance and training costs to ensure 
that employees are competent and confident in their use of the 
latest Internet and online technologies. 
Reduced productivity - Surveys from around the world have 
consistently shown that labour productivity is harmed by 
employees who regularly access personal emails and social 
media websites during working hours.

When adopting certain technologies, managers need to

Costs -
such as the cost of purchase, installation,

Benefits - such as the expected gains in efficiency (as

Economic opportunities and 
threats (STEEPLE analysis) 
The economic environment refers to the state of the economy 
in which businesses operate. This is determined by the 
government's ability to achieve its key economic objectives: (i) 
to control inflation, (ii) to reduce unemployment, (iii) to achieve 
economic growth and (iv) to achieve a healthy international 
trade balance

subject: Business Management

. Government policies used to achieve these 
fundamental goals will therefore present opportunities and 
threats for businesses. 
(i} To control inflation 
Inflation is the continual rise in the general level of prices in 
an economy. Most economists regard low and stable inflation 
as a prerequisite to achieving the other three key economic 
objectives, so this is an absolute priority for economic 
prosperity. Inflation, if not controlled, can complicate business 
planning and decision-making. For example, raw material 
costs, catalogue and menu prices and wage claims are all 
affected by inflation. Essentially, inflation that is not controlled 
becomes a threat to businesses due to the higher costs and the 
uncertainties that are caused.

Inflation also affects the international competitiveness of a 
country (see Question 46.4). An economy that has a relatively 
higher inflation rate tends to be less price-competitive when 
trading overseas. This would generally lead to a fall in export 
earnings, lower national output and higher unemployment. 
Hence, uncontrolled inflation is detrimental to businesses 
operating in the domestic economy. 
Inflation can be caused by excessive demand in the economy ( too 
much spending). Any factor that causes a rise in consumption, 
investment, government spending or international trade 
earnings will increase the economy's aggregate demand. For 
example, households and firms will spend more money and at 
a faster rate if income levels continually rise, thereby fuelling 
inflation. Alternatively, inflation can be caused by higher costs 
of production (leading to a rise in prices so that firms can 
maintain their profit margins). Examples include increased 
wages caused by trade union action, soaring prices caused by 
an energy crisis and higher rents in the economy. 
(ii} To reduce unemployment 
The unemployment rate measures the proportion of a country's 
workforce not in official employment

spending on welfare benefits for the unemployed, which means 
taxpayers have less disposable income to spend on goods and 
services. Overall, the country's international competitiveness is 
therefore likely to deteriorate.

closures since March 2020 are now permanent

(iv) To achieve a healthy international trade 
balance 
In broad terms, the internal trade balance records the value 
of a country's export earnings and its import expenditure. 
Governments strive to avoid a deficit on their international 
trade balance. This means they try to avoid the value of import 
expenditure exceeding export earnings. Just as individuals 
cannot spend more than they earn in the long run, the same 
applies to countries. 
To correct an imbalance on its international trade balance, 
governments often attempt to alter their exchange rate, 
which can provide opportunities or threats for businesses. The 
exchange rate measures the value of the domestic currency in 
terms of foreign currencies. A higher exchange rate (known 
as an appreciation of the currency) means that export prices 
will be relatively higher, thereby reducing the exporter's price 
competitiveness. Although a lower exchange rate (known as 
a depreciation of the currency) should give domestic firms a 
relative price advantage, it also means that they have to pay 
higher prices for imported raw materials and components

subject: Business Management
content:
. 
Continual and large fluctuations in exchange rates can create 
threats for businesses. Business planning and forecasting 
become very complex and perhaps impractical. For example, 
businesses may not be able to accurately forecast export sales 
or costs of imported materials due to exchange rate volatility. 
International trade deals could be postponed until the business 
626 
can benefit from more favourable movements in the exchange 
rate (although there is no guarantee that this will ever happen). 
Figure 46.7 - Fluctuations in the exchange rate affect 
business operations and profitability 
Alternatively, governments can set up international trade 
barriers to correct any disparity in its international trade 
balance or to protect their domestic industries. Protectionist 
measures refer to any government policy used to safeguard 
domestic businesses from foreign competitors (see Box 46.3). 
Such measures present threats or barriers to trade, for foreign 
businesses operating in overseas markets. 
Box 46.3 - Examples of protectionist 
measures 
Tariffs (or customs duties) are taxes on imported 
products, thereby raising their price to give domestic 
firms a price advantage. 
Quotas are quantitative limits on the volume or 
value of imports, thereby protecting their domestic 
industries

subject: Business Management
content:
. 
Subsidies are payments made by a government 
to domestic businesses as a form of financial aid 
to reduce their production costs, thereby giving 
domestic firms a competitive advantage. 
Embargos are physical bans on international trade 
with a certain country, usually due to strategic 
reasons, severe health and safety concerns or 
political conflicts. 
Technological and safety standards are strict 
administration and compliance costs in meeting 
industrial and health and safety regulations imposed 
on imported products.

Environmental opportunities and 
threats (STEEPLE analysis) 
Individuals organizations and governments are increasingly 
concerned about the negative impacts of business activity on 
the natural environment. Without government intervention, 
private sector businesses are unlikely to consider the external 
costs of business activity - the costs incurred by society rather 
than by the buyer or seller. Examples of external costs include 
passive smoking, air and noise pollution, packaging waste 
and global warming. Climate change has been blamed for the 
increase in natural disasters such as tsunamis and hurricanes. 
Changes in social attitudes towards the environment have 
meant that businesses are increasingly reviewing their practices 
and adopting various circular business models (see Chapter 51). 
Firms that do not respect the environment face ruining their 
reputation and long-term profitability. However, if compliance 
costs are too high then firms may not be able to afford more 
environmentally friendly operations. The extent to which 
businesses consider environmental issues also depends on their 
aims and objectives, the attitudes of workers and management, 
the likely impact on their profits and the available resources

Governments can also use interest rate policies to influence the 
level of business activity. The interest rate is the price of money, 
both in terms of the cost of borrowing money and the return 
for saving money in a bank account. If the economy is growing 
too fast (an economic boom), the government or the Central 
Bank is likely to raise interest rates to combat the effects of 
inflation, and vice versa. For example, in 2018, the Argentinian 
government raised interest rates to 40% in an attempt to combat 
inflation rates in excess of 25%. 
Raising interest rates makes borrowing less attractive because 
households and businesses face higher interest repayments 
on their loans. In addition, those with existing credit card 
bills, loans and mortgages face escalating interest repayments. 
Higher interest rates automatically reduce people's disposable 
income after their interest-bearing loans have been paid. 
Hence, those with existing loans or debts may need to reduce 
their overall spending. Overall, an increase in interest rates 
is likely to reduce consumption and investment expenditure, 
therefore being a threat to businesses, even though this may 
help to control inflation in the economy

For example, copyright, trademark and patent laws give

The government can also use deregulation to provide 
opportunities for businesses to prosper. Deregulation 
is the removal of government rules and regulations 
{bureaucracy) which constrain business activity within a 
particular industry. It should therefore enhance efficiency 
and encourage more competition within the industry.

Ethical opportunities and threats 
(STEEPLE analysis) 
Business ethics are the moral principles that are or should 
be, considered in business decision-making, based on what is 
judged to be right or wrong in society. Ethical firms act in a 
socially responsible way towards their stakeholders (especially 
their customers, employees and the local community), such as 
protecting the natural environment by using resources efficiently 
and minimizing waste. Ethical firms also pay their workers on 
time, do not employ workers below the legal minimum age or 
allow their employees to operate in poor working conditions. 
They do not use misleading marketing or deal with corrupt 
suppliers, sponsors or governments. 
Although there are compliance costs in acting ethically, 
businesses that are socially responsible can benefit in numerous 
ways: 
They attract and retain good quality workers - Google, for 
example, has a very loyal and dedicated workforce, partly 
because of the astonishing working environment which 
includes free buffet meals, gym access, laundry and a host 
of other on-site benefits. 
They attract new customers and retain existing ones - To 
remain competitive, businesses need to consider the impact 
of their operations on society and the environment because 
customers are increasingly concerned about environmental 
protection and ethical business behaviour

subject: Business Management
content:
. 
Behaving ethically generates good publicity and public 
relations (see Chapter 29) - Organizations such as The 
Body Shop, The Co-operative and Friends of The Earth 
have used their ethical stance to propel their business and 
mission (cause). 
Businesses are increasingly prepared to have external social 
audits conducted. These are reports on the ethical and social 
stance of a business, examined and reported by an external 
agency. The social audit reports both external matters (such 
as a firm's involvement in community projects and the level of 
pollution caused by the firm) and internal issues (such as the 
efficiency of its waste management processes and its ability to 
provide staff with a safe working environment). 
Choosing to be ethical and socially responsible can bring 
benefits, but there are also compliance costs involved with such 
decisions. A business might not always be able to pursue the 
cheapest or the most profitable option due to the costs of being 
632 
ethical and socially responsible. For example, the cheapest 
supplier might not be chosen if it is perceived (by customers 
and other stakeholders) to be an unethical business.

Cash cows are products with high market share competing

and the products are very well established (such as Coca-
Cola in the soft drinks industry or Apple's iPhone in the 
smartphone market), thereby generating remarkable net

However, some cash cows run the risk of becoming dogs,

The BCG matrix shows that the ideal product portfolio for a 
business is to have a balanced portfolio, which might include 
some stars, a few question marks and several cash cows. It is 
important to note that the BCG matrix is not a static business 
model. The money generated from cash cows is used to turn 
the question marks into stars, otherwise they may quickly 
become dogs. Similarly, stars may ultimately become cash cows. 
Appropriate marketing strategies need to be devised to foster 
these changes. Managers also need to decide whether to spend 
money on reviving the demand for dogs or to withdraw all 
investments in them, thereby releasing cash for other products. 
Hence, it is important that a business has a balanced and diverse 
range of products in its portfolio. 
A diverse product portfolio is important for an organization's 
cash flow because only selling to a single market limits the 
revenue streams of the business (see Chapter 16)

portfolio also helps to spread risks because a decline in sales for 
one product may be offset by favourable sales of other products 
in the portfolio.

KEY TERMS 
The Boston Consulting Group matrix is a situational and 
decision-making tool use for analysing the product portfolio of 
a business. It shows whether products have a high or low market 
share and operate in high or low market growth industries. 
Cash cow refers to any product in a firm's portfolio that 
generates significant money due to its large market share in a 
mature market. 
Dogs are products in the BCG matrix that have low market 
share and operate in low growth or stagnant markets. Hence, 
dogs do not generate much cash or profit for a business. 
Question marks ( or wild cards) are products in the BCG matrix 
that compete in high market growth industries but have low 
market share. They consume lots of cash but do not generate 
much profit, if any

market share in a high growth market. They have the potential 
to become cash cows if funded and marketed appropriately.

Many business plans have sections devoted to a SWOT analysis 
(see Chapter 44) and a contingency plan (see Chapter 41) 
outlining what the entrepreneur will do if things do not go as 
planned. Finally, any appropriate supporting evidence (such as 
statistics, charts and other reference material) should appear in 
an appendix at the back of the business plan. 
Business plans are particularly important for business start-ups 
(see Chapter 1). Poor cash flow management (see Chapter 20) is 
one of the main causes of business failure. Hence, it is common 
for a new business to include a cash flow forecast in the business 
plan so that provisions can be made to cover any shortfalls. 
As bank managers are busy people, a typical business plan is 
often no more than 5 to 6 pages long. If this is not possible, such 
as in the case of a proposal for an international joint venture, 
then an executive summary is written and placed at the front 
of the business plan. This summarises the information given 
in the main report of the business plan, highlighting the key 
points and conclusions. The executive summary can be read 
within a few minutes to get an overview of the business plan 
and the bank manager can then decide whether or not to read 
the rest of the document

Evaluation of business plans 
Business plans are important as a management planning tool 
as they form a strategic focus. In particular, start-ups and small 
businesses need to focus on their unique identities, target 
markets and their goods or services tailored to match the needs 
and wants of the market. 
Furthermore, a business plan provides a framework or structure 
as a planning tool to keep the business focused on its goals 
and objectives. Used appropriately and referred to regularly, 
a business plan helps decision makers and entrepreneurs to 
manage their priorities and different areas of focus. 
Business plans can also be important for managing change in 
business organizations. With good planning, decision makers 
and entrepreneurs regularly review key performance indicators 
(such as sales growth or market share data), track progress and 
pursue new business opportunities. Business plans provide 
a detailed and structured roadmap, which can be adjusted if 
needed, thereby helping to improve the chances of commercial 
success
